Domino Tilings, Domino Shuffling, and the Nabla Operator

Ian Cavey ††thanks: cavey@illinois.edu Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL, USA    Yi-Lin Lee ††thanks: yillee@iu.edu Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN, USA
Abstract

We study domino tilings of certain regions RλR_{\lambda}, indexed by partitions λ\lambda, weighted according to generalized area and dinv statistics. These statistics arise from the q,tq,t-Catalan combinatorics and Macdonald polynomials. We present a formula for the generating polynomial of these domino tilings in terms of the Bergeron–Garsia nabla operator. When λ=(nn)\lambda=(n^{n}) is a square shape, domino tilings of RλR_{\lambda} are equivalent to those of the Aztec diamond of order nn. In this case, we give a new product formula for the resulting polynomials by domino shuffling and its connection with alternating sign matrices. In particular, we obtain a combinatorial proof of the joint symmetry of the generalized area and dinv statistics.

Keywords. Alternating sign matrices; domino tilings; domino shuffling; nabla operator; q,tq,t-Catalan combinatorics; symmetric functions.

2020 Mathematics Subject Classification. 05A15, 05A19, 05B45, 05E05.

1 Introduction

The study of Macdonald polynomials has produced many interesting combinatorial objects, often expressed as weighted sums over sets of lattice paths. Perhaps the most famous and well-studied such objects are the q,tq,t-Catalan numbers introduced by Garsia and Haiman [9], which can be defined combinatorially as the sum over Dyck paths weighted by the area and dinv statistics (see the book [11] and the references therein). Among the many generalizations of the q,tq,t-Catalan numbers are the extension to Schröder paths defined by Egge, Haglund, Killpatrick, and Kremer [5], and to nested families of Dyck paths due to Loehr and Warrington [13]. All of these objects have natural interpretations in terms of Macdonald polynomials often expressed via the nabla operator ∇\nabla on symmetric functions introduced by Bergeron and Garsia [1]. In this paper, we study the common generalization to nested families of Schröder paths and their connection to domino tilings.

Let Λ\Lambda denote the ring of symmetric functions in the countably infinite set of variables {xi}i≥1\{x_{i}\}_{i\geq 1} with coefficients in the field of rational functions ℚ⁡(q,t).\mathbb{Q}(q,t). We will make use of the Hall inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle on Λ\Lambda, and the following vector space bases for Λ\Lambda, each indexed by partitions μ\mu: the monomial symmetric functions mμm_{\mu}, the elementary symmetric functions eμe_{\mu}, the complete homogeneous symmetric functions hμh_{\mu}, the Schur functions sμs_{\mu}, and the modified Macdonald Polynomials H~μ\tilde{H}_{\mu}. For details on the classical bases and the Hall inner product, see the book [15]. The modified Macdonald polynomials H~μ\tilde{H}_{\mu} are variants of the polynomials studied by Macdonald [16] appearing in Garsia and Haiman’s work on diagonal harmonics [9]. See also [11, Chapter 2] for more details.

The nabla operator is the unique ℚ⁡(q,t)\mathbb{Q}(q,t)-linear map ∇\nabla on Λ\Lambda such that

∇(H~μ)=qn⁡(μ′)​tn⁡(μ)​H~μ,\nabla(\tilde{H}_{\mu})=q^{n(\mu^{\prime})}t^{n(\mu)}\tilde{H}_{\mu}, (1)

for all μ\mu, where μ′\mu^{\prime} is the conjugate of μ\mu and n⁡(μ)=∑(i−1)​μin(\mu)=\sum(i-1)\mu_{i}. One can obtain interesting combinatorial objects by applying ∇\nabla to elements of some basis of Λ\Lambda and expanding the result in terms of another bases or, equivalently, taking the inner product with an element of the dual basis. We list some of these combinatorial objects in Table 1. For other formulas of this kind, see [13].

Let λ=(λ1,…,λℓ)\lambda=(\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{\ell}) be a partition of nn where n=λ1+⋯+λℓn=\lambda_{1}+\cdots+\lambda_{\ell} and λ1≥λ2≥⋯≥λℓ>0\lambda_{1}\geq\lambda_{2}\geq\cdots\geq\lambda_{\ell}>0. We identify λ\lambda with its Ferrers diagram (in English notation) as in Figure 1. Loehr and Warrington [13] consider strictly nested collections of Dyck paths with starting points (0,0),(1,1),(2,2)​…(0,0),(1,1),(2,2)\dots, and ending points determined by λ\lambda in the following way. Decompose the Ferrers diagram of λ\lambda into border strips and label each column with the length of the strip whose rightmost box is in that column (and with label 00 if there is no such strip) as shown in Figure 1 for the partition λ=(4,4,3,3,3,1)\lambda=(4,4,3,3,3,1). Let n0,…,nkn_{0},\dots,n_{k} denote these labels read from right to left where k=λ1−1k=\lambda_{1}-1. A λ\lambda-family of Dyck paths is a (k+1)(k+1)-tuple π=(π0,…,πk)\pi=(\pi_{0},\dots,\pi_{k}) of pairwise non-intersecting lattice paths, where each πj\pi_{j} is a lattice path consisting of unit north (0,1)(0,1) and east (1,0)(1,0) steps that lies weakly above the diagonal y=xy=x, starts at (j,j)(j,j), and ends at (j+nj,j+nj)(j+n_{j},j+n_{j}).

In this paper we study the Schröder generalization of these nested families of paths. Using the same notation as for the Dyck paths, a λ\lambda-family of Schröder paths is a (k+1)(k+1)-tuple π=(π0,…,πk)\pi=(\pi_{0},\dots,\pi_{k}) of pairwise non-intersecting lattice paths, where each πi\pi_{i} is a lattice path consisting of unit north (0,1)(0,1), east (1,0)(1,0), and diagonal (1,1)(1,1) steps that lies weakly above the diagonal y=xy=x, starts at (j,j)(j,j), and ends at (j+nj,j+nj)(j+n_{j},j+n_{j}). Figure 1 shows a λ\lambda-family of paths for the partition in Figure 1. Let 𝒮λ\mathcal{S}_{\lambda} be the set of all λ\lambda-families of Schröder paths and 𝒮λ,d\mathcal{S}_{\lambda,d} the set of all λ\lambda-families of Schröder paths with dd total diagonal steps among all the paths.

We define generalized area and dinv statistics on 𝒮λ,d\mathcal{S}_{\lambda,d} (Section 2.1) that specialize to the corresponding statistics in the cases of λ\lambda-families of Dyck paths, (single) Schröder paths, and (single) Dyck paths. In the rest of the paper, we refer to generalized area and dinv statistics simply as area and dinv.

Our first result expresses λ\lambda-families of Schröder paths weighted according to these statistics in the language of Macdonald polynomials. In the following formula, 𝗌𝗀𝗇⁡(λ)=±1\sgn(\lambda)=\pm 1 is a sign factor introduced in [13] whose definition is recalled in Section 2.1.

Theorem 1.1.

For any partition λ⊢n\lambda\vdash n and 0≤d≤n0\leq d\leq n,

∑π∈𝒮λ,dq𝖺𝗋𝖾𝖺⁡(π)​t𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏⁡(π)=𝗌𝗀𝗇⁡(λ)​⟨∇(sλ),hd​en−d⟩.\sum_{\pi\in\mathcal{S}_{\lambda,d}}q^{\area(\pi)}t^{\dinv(\pi)}=\sgn(\lambda)\langle\nabla(s_{\lambda}),h_{d}\,e_{n-d}\rangle. (2)

Theorem 1.1 is the common generalization of several formulas relating q,tq,t-Catalan combinatorics to Macdonald polynomials through the ∇\nabla operator summarized in Table 1. When d=0d=0, (2) reduces to the formula 𝗌𝗀𝗇⁡(λ)​⟨∇(sλ),en⟩\sgn(\lambda)\langle\nabla(s_{\lambda}),e_{n}\rangle for λ\lambda-families of Dyck paths. When λ=(1n)\lambda=(1^{n}), one recovers the formula ⟨∇(en),hd​en−d⟩\langle\nabla(e_{n}),h_{d}\,e_{n-d}\rangle for the q,tq,t-Schröder numbers. In the intersection of these cases, when d=0d=0 and λ=(1n)\lambda=(1^{n}), the formula ⟨∇(en),en⟩\langle\nabla(e_{n}),e_{n}\rangle gives the q,tq,t-Catalan numbers.

We obtain Theorem 1.1 from an even more general formula for the full monomial expansion of ∇(sλ)\nabla(s_{\lambda}) in terms of labeled weakly-nested Dyck paths introduced by Loehr and Warrington [13] and recently proved by Blasiak, Haiman, Morse, Pun, and Seelinger [2]. Our proof of Theorem 1.1 in Section 3 closely follows Haglund’s argument to obtain the corresponding formula for (single) Schröder paths from the shuffle formula for (single) labeled Dyck paths from the Superization section of [11, Chapter 6].

Our present interest in these polynomials is due to a general bijection [14] between domino tilings11 1 A domino tiling of RR is a covering of RR using dominoes (1×21\times 2 or 2×12\times 1 rectangles) without gaps or overlaps. of regions RR on the square lattice and families of non-intersecting Schröder-like paths contained in RR (see Section 2.3). Motivated by this bijection, we define below a region RλR_{\lambda} whose domino tilings correspond to λ\lambda-families of Schröder paths in the set 𝒮λ\mathcal{S}_{\lambda}. This region is related to the Aztec diamond introduced by Elkies, Kuperberg, Larsen, and Propp [6, 7] in 1992. One goal of this project is to establish a bridge between the rich combinatorics surrounding domino tilings of the Aztec diamond (and similar regions) and q,tq,t-Catalan combinatorics.

The Aztec diamond of order nn, denoted by ADn\AD_{n}, is the union of all unit squares inside the diamond-shaped region {(x,y)∈ℝ2:|x|+|y|≤n+1}\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}:|x|+|y|\leq n+1\}. Given a partition λ\lambda decomposed into border strips of lengths (n0,…,nk)(n_{0},\dots,n_{k}) as above, RλR_{\lambda} will be defined as a certain subset of the top half, y≥0y\geq 0, of ADn0+1\AD_{n_{0}+1}. To describe this region, equip the Aztec diamond with the checkerboard coloring so that the unit squares along the top right side are colored black. Label the boxes in the bottom row of the top half of the Aztec diamond 0,0,1,1,2,2,…,n0,n00,0,1,1,2,2,\dots,n_{0},n_{0} from left to right. The region RλR_{\lambda} is defined by removing from this region the white boxes in the bottom row labeled 0,1,…,k0,1,\dots,k and the black boxes in the bottom row labeled i+nii+n_{i} for each i=0,…,ki=0,\dots,k. Let 𝒯⁡(Rλ)\T(R_{\lambda}) be the set of domino tilings of RλR_{\lambda}. As explained in Section 2.3, 𝒯⁡(Rλ)\T(R_{\lambda}) is in bijection with 𝒮λ\mathcal{S}_{\lambda}. Figure 1 shows the domino tiling of RλR_{\lambda} corresponding to the λ\lambda-family in Figure 1.

Passing through this bijection, we define in Section 2.3 statistics 𝖺𝗋𝖾𝖺\area, 𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏\dinv, and 𝖽𝗂𝖺𝗀𝗌\diags directly on 𝒯⁡(Rλ)\T(R_{\lambda}) that agree with the corresponding statistics on 𝒮λ,d\mathcal{S}_{\lambda,d}. We then study the following generating polynomial of domino tilings of RλR_{\lambda}, where λ\lambda is a partition of nn:

Pλ​(z,q,t):=∑T∈𝒯⁡(Rλ)z𝖽𝗂𝖺𝗀𝗌⁡(T)​q𝖺𝗋𝖾𝖺⁡(T)​t𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏⁡(T)=∑d=0n∑π∈𝒮λ,dzd​q𝖺𝗋𝖾𝖺⁡(π)​t𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏⁡(π).P_{\lambda}(z;q,t):=\sum_{T\in\T(R_{\lambda})}z^{\diags(T)}q^{\area(T)}t^{\dinv(T)}=\sum_{d=0}^{n}\sum_{\pi\in\mathcal{S}_{\lambda,d}}z^{d}q^{\area(\pi)}t^{\dinv(\pi)}. (3)

A consequence of Theorem 1.1 is the symmetry of Pλ​(z,q,t)P_{\lambda}(z;q,t) in the variables qq and tt.

Corollary 1.2.

For all partitions λ\lambda, we have Pλ​(z,q,t)=Pλ​(z,t,q)P_{\lambda}(z;q,t)=P_{\lambda}(z;t,q).

The proof of Corollary 1.2 is also found in Section 3. As is often the case in q,tq,t-Catalan combinatorics, we do not have a combinatorial proof the joint symmetry of the area and dinv statistics in general.

A special role is played by the partitions of square shape, λ=(nn)\lambda=(n^{n}), in which case domino tilings of RλR_{\lambda} are in bijection with domino tilings ADn\AD_{n} (see Section 4.1). For convenience, we write

ADn⁡(z,q,t)=P(nn)​(z,q,t).\AD_{n}(z;q,t)=P_{(n^{n})}(z;q,t). (4)

Surprisingly, the combinatorics of alternating sign matrices and domino shuffling introduced in [6, 7] interact well with the statistics 𝖺𝗋𝖾𝖺\area, 𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏\dinv and 𝖽𝗂𝖺𝗀𝗌\diags coming from q,tq,t-Catalan combinatorics. We use this machinery to prove the following product formula for ADn⁡(z,q,t)\AD_{n}(z;q,t).

Theorem 1.3.

When λ=(nn)\lambda=(n^{n}) is a partition of square shape, then

ADn⁡(z,q,t)=(q​t)n2​(n−1)/2​∏i,j≥0​ and ​i+j<n(z+qi​tj).\AD_{n}(z;q,t)=(qt)^{n^{2}(n-1)/2}\prod_{i,j\geq 0\text{ and }i+j<n}(z+q^{i}t^{j}). (5)

Specializing all variables to 11, we recover the well-known fact that the number of domino tilings of ADn\AD_{n} is 2n⁡(n+1)/22^{n(n+1)/2}. This product formula is similar to the formula given in [6, 7] weighted according to different statistics. Specifically, our statistic 𝖽𝗂𝖺𝗀𝗌⁡(T)\diags(T) is the same as their statistic v⁡(T)v(T) counting vertical dominoes up to a simple change of variables. Our 𝖺𝗋𝖾𝖺⁡(T)\area(T) statistic is similar to their rank statistic r⁡(T)r(T), although they are not the same, and our 𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏⁡(T)\dinv(T) statistic appears to be completely new. In the recent work [4], Corteel, Gitlin, and Keating introduced kk-tilings (kk-tuples of domino tilings) of ADn\AD_{n} and computed their generating polynomials. One of the statistics they considered is based on the number of “coupled dominoes” (see [4, Section 2.4]), which is analogues to our “domino pairs” (see Figure 6), although the two concepts are different.

Our proof of Theorem 1.3 is entirely combinatorial and the formula is evidently symmetric in qq and tt, so we in particular obtain a direct proof (not using Theorem 1.1) of the q,tq,t-symmetry in Corollary 1.2 for partitions of square shape.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we define statistics on λ\lambda-families of Schröder paths and domino tilings, and state some background information on related combinatorics of alternating sign matrices and domino shuffling. In Section 3, we prove Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2. In Section 4, we discuss the special case when λ=(nn)\lambda=(n^{n}) and prove Theorem 1.3. In Section 5, we propose a conjecture regarding the divisibility of Pλ​(z,q,t)P_{\lambda}(z;q,t).

2 Preliminaries

We begin this section by defining the statistics on λ\lambda-families of Schröder paths 𝒮λ\mathcal{S}_{\lambda} (Section 2.1). In Section 2.2, we present the Loehr–Warrington formula which will be used to prove Theorem 1.1. In Section 2.3, we introduce the bijection between domino tilings of RλR_{\lambda} and 𝒮λ\mathcal{S}_{\lambda} and then interpret these statistics defined in Section 2.1 in terms of dominoes. Finally, we review the relation between alternating sign matrices and domino tilings of the Aztec diamond (Section 2.4) and the domino shuffling algorithm (Section 2.5).

2.1 Statistics on λ\lambda-families of Schröder paths

We define statistics on λ\lambda-families of Schröder paths building upon the statistics for Schröder paths [5] and λ\lambda-families of Dyck paths [13]. Let λ=(λ1,…,λℓ)\lambda=(\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{\ell}) be a partition. As stated in Section 1, we decompose λ\lambda by removing successive border strips, and let nj=nj​(λ)n_{j}=n_{j}(\lambda) denote the number of squares in the border strip ending at the jjth box from the right (indexed from j=0j=0) in the top row.

The dinv adjustment of λ\lambda is defined to be the quantity 𝖺𝖽𝗃(λ)=∑j:nj>0(λ1−1−j)\adj(\lambda)=\sum_{j:n_{j}>0}(\lambda_{1}-1-j) and we set22 2 The definitions of 𝖺𝖽𝗃\adj and 𝗌𝗀𝗇\sgn differ slightly from, but are equivalent to, those in [13]. 𝗌𝗀𝗇⁡(λ)=(−1)𝖺𝖽𝗃⁡(λ)\sgn(\lambda)=(-1)^{\adj(\lambda)}. In fact, 𝖺𝖽𝗃⁡(λ)\adj(\lambda) is the total number of times a border strip in the decomposition of λ\lambda crosses a vertical boundary of a unit square in λ\lambda. In the example λ=(4,4,3,3,3,1)\lambda=(4,4,3,3,3,1) depicted in Figure 1, 𝖺𝖽𝗃⁡(λ)=3+2+0=5\adj(\lambda)=3+2+0=5 and 𝗌𝗀𝗇⁡(λ)=−1\sgn(\lambda)=-1.

As defined in the introduction, a λ\lambda-family of Schröder paths in 𝒮λ\mathcal{S}_{\lambda} is a sequence π=(π0,…,πk)\pi=(\pi_{0},\dots,\pi_{k}) where k=λ1−1k=\lambda_{1}-1, such that

  1. 1.

    πj\pi_{j} is a lattice path consisting of north (0,1)(0,1) steps, east (1,0)(1,0) steps, and diagonal (1,1)(1,1) steps starting at (j,j)(j,j) and ending at (j+nj,j+nj)(j+n_{j},j+n_{j}), which never goes strictly below the diagonal y=xy=x, and

  2. 2.

    no two distinct paths πi\pi_{i} and πj\pi_{j} intersect.

Note that the construction of the vector (n0,…,nk)(n_{0},\dots,n_{k}) encoding the sizes of border strips removed from λ\lambda ensures that there exists a λ\lambda-family of Schröder paths for any partition λ\lambda.

Given π=(π0,…,πk)∈𝒮λ\pi=(\pi_{0},\dots,\pi_{k})\in\mathcal{S}_{\lambda}, we now define the first statistic

𝖽𝗂𝖺𝗀𝗌⁡(π)=∑j=0k𝖽𝗂𝖺𝗀𝗌⁡(πj),\diags(\pi)=\sum_{j=0}^{k}\diags(\pi_{j}), (6)

where 𝖽𝗂𝖺𝗀𝗌⁡(πj)\diags(\pi_{j}) is the number of diagonal (1,1)(1,1) steps in the path πj\pi_{j}. We write 𝒮λ,d\mathcal{S}_{\lambda,d} for the subset of 𝒮λ\mathcal{S}_{\lambda} consisting of λ\lambda-families π\pi with 𝖽𝗂𝖺𝗀𝗌⁡(π)=d\diags(\pi)=d. For example, the λ\lambda-family of Schröder paths π\pi in Figure 1 has 𝖽𝗂𝖺𝗀𝗌⁡(π)=2+2+1=5.\diags(\pi)=2+2+1=5.

In order to define the other statistics on these families, we encode the paths by an array following the notation for λ\lambda-families of Dyck paths [13], with added decorations to encode the diagonal steps. A triangle with vertices (c,d)(c,d), (c+1,d)(c+1,d) and (c+1,d+1)(c+1,d+1) for some integers cc and dd is called an area triangle. Given π=(π0,…,πk)∈𝒮λ\pi=(\pi_{0},\dots,\pi_{k})\in\mathcal{S}_{\lambda} and j=0,1,…,kj=0,1,\dots,k, we define ai(j)=ai(j)​(π)a^{(j)}_{i}=a^{(j)}_{i}(\pi) for each j≤i≤j+nj−1j\leq i\leq j+n_{j}-1 to be the number of area triangles in the region bounded below by y=iy=i, bounded above by y=i+1y=i+1, bounded to the left by πj\pi_{j}, and bounded to the right by y=xy=x. For values of ii outside of this range, ai(j)a^{(j)}_{i} is undefined. For each ii in this range, πj\pi_{j} has either a single north step or a single diagonal step in the row bounded by y=iy=i and y=i+1y=i+1. For the ii’s for which πj\pi_{j} has a diagonal step, we decorate ai(j)a^{(j)}_{i} with an overline. This collection of decorated numbers is called the area array of π\pi, and completely encodes the family of paths.

We define the second statistic on π=(π0,…,πk)∈𝒮λ\pi=(\pi_{0},\dots,\pi_{k})\in\mathcal{S}_{\lambda} as follows:

𝖺𝗋𝖾𝖺⁡(π)=∑j=0k𝖺𝗋𝖾𝖺⁡(πj),\area(\pi)=\sum_{j=0}^{k}\area(\pi_{j}), (7)

where 𝖺𝗋𝖾𝖺⁡(πj)\area(\pi_{j}) is the total number of area triangles below πj\pi_{j} and above the diagonal y=xy=x. In other words, 𝖺𝗋𝖾𝖺⁡(π)\area(\pi) is the sum of all the entries in the area array of π\pi, ignoring any decorations.

The λ\lambda-family of Schröder paths π\pi depicted in Figure 1 has the following area array, where ⋅\cdot denotes an undefined value. One can check that 𝖺𝗋𝖾𝖺⁡(π)=27+11+0=38\area(\pi)=27+11+0=38.

i:012345678a(0):0123455¯43¯a(1):⋅0123¯32¯⋅⋅a(2):⋅⋅⋅⋅⋅⋅⋅⋅⋅a(3):⋅⋅⋅000¯⋅⋅⋅\begin{array}[]{cccccccccc}i:&0&1&2&3&4&5&6&7&8\\ a^{(0)}:&0&1&2&3&4&5&\overline{5}&4&\overline{3}\\ a^{(1)}:&\cdot&0&1&2&\overline{3}&3&\overline{2}&\cdot&\cdot\\ a^{(2)}:&\cdot&\cdot&\cdot&\cdot&\cdot&\cdot&\cdot&\cdot&\cdot\\ a^{(3)}:&\cdot&\cdot&\cdot&0&0&\overline{0}&\cdot&\cdot&\cdot\\ \end{array}

To define our last statistic, the dinv statistic, we designate certain pairs of steps in the paths π∈𝒮λ\pi\in\mathcal{S}_{\lambda} to be dinv pairs, and record the total number of such pairs. It is more convenient to define these pairs directly from the area array, where we associate each entry ai(j)a^{(j)}_{i} with the north or diagonal step (depending on whether or not the entry is decorated) of the path πj\pi_{j} in the region i≤y≤i+1i\leq y\leq i+1. We say that a pair of entries ab(u)a^{(u)}_{b} and ac(v)a^{(v)}_{c} in the area array of π\pi is a dinv pair in π\pi if either of the following two cases hold:

  1. Case 1. ab(u)=ac(v)a^{(u)}_{b}=a^{(v)}_{c} with b<cb<c and ab(u)a^{(u)}_{b} is not decorated, or

  2. Case 2. ab(u)=ac(v)+1a^{(u)}_{b}=a^{(v)}_{c}+1 with b≤cb\leq c and ac(v)a^{(v)}_{c} is not decorated.

For equalities of entries in the area array in the conditions above, we consider only the numerical values and ignore any decorations. We then define the dinv statistic of π∈𝒮λ\pi\in\mathcal{S}_{\lambda} to be the quantity

𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏⁡(π)=𝖺𝖽𝗃⁡(λ)+|{dinv pairs in ​π}|.\dinv(\pi)=\adj(\lambda)+\left|\{\text{dinv pairs in }\pi\}\right|. (8)

Our running example π\pi in Figure 1 has 𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏⁡(π)=5+29=34\dinv(\pi)=5+29=34.

Moreover, we can interpret and visualize dinv pairs as pairs of north or diagonal steps in some, possibly different, paths in π∈𝒮λ\pi\in\mathcal{S}_{\lambda} as described above. Figure 2 depicts the possible arrangements of pairs of steps that correspond to dinv pairs. The dotted lines indicate the alignment of the pairs of steps relative to some translation of the diagonal y=xy=x.

These statistics are the common generalization of those defined for single Schröder paths and for nested Dyck paths. In the case λ=(1,1,…,1)\lambda=(1,1,\dots,1), a λ\lambda-family of Schröder paths reduces to a single Schröder path, and the statistics we have defined above coincide with those for single Schröder paths [5]. On the other hand, if π∈𝒮λ,d\pi\in\mathcal{S}_{\lambda,d} with d=0d=0, then it can be considered as a λ\lambda-family of Dyck paths and the area and dinv statistics above coincide with those defined in [13]. Both of these cases specialize further to π∈𝒮λ,d\pi\in\mathcal{S}_{\lambda,d} for λ=(1,1,…,1)\lambda=(1,1,\dots,1) and d=0d=0, that is, single Dyck paths, in which case these statistics recover the area and dinv statistics for the q,tq,t-Catalan numbers [8].

2.2 The Loehr–Warrington Formula

The Loehr–Warrington formula gives the full monomial expansion of ∇(sλ)\nabla(s_{\lambda}) for any partition λ\lambda as a weighted sum over labeled, weakly-nested λ\lambda-families of Dyck paths. It was conjectured by Loehr and Warrington [13, Conjecture 2.1] and proved recently by Blasiak, Haiman, Morse, Pun, and Seelinger [2]. We recall the definition of these objects and their statistics below informally. See [13, Section 2.3] for the precise definitions in terms of area and label arrays. A weakly-nested λ\lambda-families of Dyck paths is a collection of paths π=(π0,π1,…,πk)\pi=(\pi_{0},\pi_{1},\dots,\pi_{k}) where k=λ1−1k=\lambda_{1}-1, such that

  1. 1.

    Each path πj\pi_{j} is a lattice path from (j,j)(j,j) to (j+nj,j+nj)(j+n_{j},j+n_{j}) made up of north (0,1)(0,1) steps and east (1,0)(1,0) steps that never goes below the diagonal y=xy=x,

  2. 2.

    two distinct paths πi\pi_{i} and πj\pi_{j} can never cross and can never share east steps but may touch and may share north steps, and

  3. 3.

    no path πj\pi_{j} meets the starting point of any other path πi\pi_{i}.

A labeling of a weakly-nested λ\lambda-family of Dyck paths is an assignment of a positive integer to each north step in all the paths of the family such that

  1. 1.

    On any sequence of consecutive north steps of any path πj\pi_{j}, the labels on these north steps strictly increase from bottom to top, and

  2. 2.

    whenever there is a north steps labeled rr directly below a north step labeled r′r^{\prime} (i.e. the ending point of the north step labeled rr is the starting point of the north step labeled r′r^{\prime}) on some paths πi\pi_{i} and πj\pi_{j} respectively with j<ij<i, we have r′≤rr^{\prime}\leq r.

Let LNDPλ\LNDP_{\lambda} denote the set of all pairs (π,w)(\pi,w) where π\pi is a weakly-nested λ\lambda-family of Dyck paths with labeling ww. An example of a labeled weakly-nested λ\lambda-family of Dyck paths is shown in Figure 3, with labels on the outermost path appearing on the left of the corresponding edge, and labels on the other paths on the right.

The area of a Dyck path is the number of complete unit boxes (or equivalently the number of area triangles, as defined in Section 2.1) underneath the path and above the diagonal y=xy=x. The area of a weakly-nested λ\lambda-family of Dyck paths is the sum of the areas of the paths in the family. For a family π\pi with labeling ww, the statistic 𝖺𝗋𝖾𝖺⁡(π,w)\area(\pi,w) is defined as the area of the family π\pi, not depending on the labeling of the family. For example, the area of the λ\lambda-family in Figure 3 is 1414.

The dinv statistic of a labeled family, however, does depend on the labeling. Let (π,w)∈LNDPλ(\pi,w)\in\LNDP_{\lambda} and N1N_{1} and N2N_{2} be any two north steps from any paths in π\pi with distinct labels L1L_{1} and L2L_{2} respectively, where L1<L2L_{1}<L_{2}. We say that this pair is a dinv pair for (π,w)(\pi,w) if either of the following conditions hold:

  1. 1.

    The north steps are on the same diagonal (some line y=x+cy=x+c meets the bottom-most points of both N1N_{1} and N2N_{2}) and N2N_{2} lies weakly to the left of N1N_{1}.

  2. 2.

    There is some line y=x+cy=x+c that meets the top-most point of N2N_{2} and the bottom-most point of N1N_{1}, and N2N_{2} lies strictly to the left of N1N_{1}.

Figure 4 shows two families of pairs of vertical steps that are dinv pairs for any labeling with a<ba<b.

For any pair (π,w)∈LNDPλ(\pi,w)\in\LNDP_{\lambda}, define the statistic 𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏⁡(π,w)=𝖺𝖽𝗃⁡(λ)+|{dinv pairs in ​(π,w)}|\dinv(\pi,w)=\adj(\lambda)+\left|\{\text{dinv pairs in }(\pi,w)\}\right|. For example, the labeled family in Figure 3 has 𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏⁡(π,w)=5+14=19\dinv(\pi,w)=5+14=19. Finally, let xwx^{w} denote the monomial in the variables {xi}i≥1\{x_{i}\}_{i\geq 1} such that the exponent on each xix_{i} is the number of ii’s that appear in the labeling ww.

The following theorem presents the Loehr–Warrington formula, it will be used to prove Theorem 1.1 later in Section 3.

Theorem 2.1 ([13] and [2]).

For any partition λ\lambda,

∇(sλ)=𝗌𝗀𝗇⁡(λ)​∑(π,w)∈LNDPλq𝖺𝗋𝖾𝖺⁡(π,w)​t𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏⁡(π,w)​xw.\nabla(s_{\lambda})=\sgn(\lambda)\sum_{(\pi,w)\in\LNDP_{\lambda}}q^{\area(\pi,w)}t^{\dinv(\pi,w)}x^{w}. (9)

2.3 Bijection between Domino Tilings and Schröder-like Paths

In general, there is a bijection [14] between domino tilings of a region RR on the square lattice and families of non-intersecting paths contained in RR. In particular, domino tilings of RλR_{\lambda} are in bijection with λ\lambda-families of Schröder paths. This bijection is described below.

Given a domino tiling of RλR_{\lambda}, the corresponding family of paths is given by decorating each of the four types of dominoes that can appear relative to the checkerboard coloring with a (possibly empty) path step as shown in Figure 5. Regarding each of these path steps as oriented from left to right, each step enters a domino in a black square and exits a domino in a white square. The union of all of these individual path steps therefore forms a collection of non-intersecting paths in RλR_{\lambda}. The starting points of these paths are the black squares in RλR_{\lambda} such that the white square immediately to its left is not in RλR_{\lambda} and the ending points of these paths are the white squares in RλR_{\lambda} such that the black square immediately to its right is not in RλR_{\lambda}.

One can view the resulting family of paths as λ\lambda-family of Schröder paths by a change of coordinates that amounts to rotating 45∘45^{\circ} counterclockwise and rescaling so that the longest path begins at (0,0)(0,0) and ends at (n0,n0)(n_{0},n_{0}). More precisely, the corresponding λ\lambda-family of Schröder paths is the image of the paths in RλR_{\lambda} under the unique affine transformation that takes the points (−n0,1/2),(0,n0+1/2),(-n_{0},1/2),(0,n_{0}+1/2), and (n0,1/2)(n_{0},1/2) to (0,0),(0,n0),(0,0),(0,n_{0}), and (n0,n0)(n_{0},n_{0}), respectively. See Figures 1 and 1. Conversely, given a λ\lambda-family of Schröder paths, we can undo the affine transformation above to obtain a family of paths in RλR_{\lambda}. We then cover RλR_{\lambda} with dominoes based on the four configurations in Figure 5. This gives the corresponding domino tiling of RλR_{\lambda}.

Next, we explain how to express the statistics defined in Section 2.1 from the viewpoint of domino tilings of RλR_{\lambda}. Given a domino tiling T∈𝒯⁡(Rλ)T\in\T(R_{\lambda}) and its corresponding λ\lambda-family of Schröder paths π∈𝒮λ\pi\in\mathcal{S}_{\lambda}. Let V⁡(T)V(T) (resp., H⁡(T)H(T)) be the collection of all vertical (resp., horizontal) dominoes in which the bottom (resp., left) unit square is colored black. These two particular types of domino correspond to the up and diagonal steps in π\pi. For convenience, we also write Vc​(T)V^{c}(T) (resp., Hc​(T)H^{c}(T)) for the collection of all vertical (resp., horizontal) dominoes in which the top (resp., right) unit square is colored black.

One can easily see that the diags statistic is given by 𝖽𝗂𝖺𝗀𝗌⁡(π)=𝖽𝗂𝖺𝗀𝗌⁡(T)=|H⁡(T)|\diags(\pi)=\diags(T)=|H(T)|.

Recall that the area statistic counts the total number of area triangles of each path in π\pi. This can be expressed as a sum over the “area” of each vertical domino in V⁡(T)V(T) and horizontal domino in H⁡(T)H(T), where each area contribution depends on the yy-coordinate of that domino. To be more precise, for a vertical domino dv∈V⁡(T)d_{v}\in V(T) and a horizontal domino dh∈H⁡(T)d_{h}\in H(T) whose bottom edge lies on y=iy=i, (0≤i≤n0)(0\leq i\leq n_{0}), define 𝖺𝗋𝖾𝖺⁡(dv)=𝖺𝗋𝖾𝖺⁡(dh)=i\area(d_{v})=\area(d_{h})=i. Then the area statistic can be reinterpreted as

𝖺𝗋𝖾𝖺⁡(π)=𝖺𝗋𝖾𝖺⁡(T)=∑dv∈V⁡(T)𝖺𝗋𝖾𝖺⁡(dv)+∑dh∈H⁡(T)𝖺𝗋𝖾𝖺⁡(dh).\area(\pi)=\area(T)=\sum_{d_{v}\in V(T)}\area(d_{v})+\sum_{d_{h}\in H(T)}\area(d_{h}). (10)

The dinv pairs defined for λ\lambda-families of Schröder paths (Figure 2) are equivalent to the domino pairs shown in Figure 6. Hence, the dinv statistic can be expressed as

𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏⁡(π)=𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏⁡(T)=𝖺𝖽𝗃⁡(λ)+|{domino pairs in ​T}|.\dinv(\pi)=\dinv(T)=\adj(\lambda)+\left|\{\text{domino pairs in }T\}\right|. (11)

The number of domino pairs in TT can be expressed as a sum over the “dinv” of each vertical domino dvd_{v} in V⁡(T)V(T), there are two ways to define the dinv statistic on dvd_{v} based on the reference vertical domino (type I or type II) shown in each configuration of domino pairs (Figure 6).

For the type I reference domino dvd_{v}, we define 𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏1⁡(dv)\dinv_{1}(d_{v}) to be the number of these four kinds of dominoes (two on the left and two on the right of dvd_{v}) aligning in the way shown in Figure 6. To the left of dvd_{v}, we count the number of horizontal dominoes in H⁡(T)H(T) aligning with the top unit square of dvd_{v}, and vertical dominoes in V⁡(T)V(T) whose bottom unit square is aligned with the bottom unit square of dvd_{v}; to the right of dvd_{v}, we count the number of horizontal dominoes in H⁡(T)H(T) aligning with the bottom unit square of dvd_{v}, and vertical dominoes in V⁡(T)V(T) whose top unit square is aligned with the bottom unit square of dvd_{v}. Then 𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏1⁡(dv)\dinv_{1}(d_{v}) is the sum of these two quantities mentioned above. Summing 𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏1⁡(dv)\dinv_{1}(d_{v}) over all the vertical dominoes in V⁡(T)V(T) gives the number of domino pairs in TT.

Similarly, for the type II reference domino dvd_{v}, 𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏2⁡(dv)\dinv_{2}(d_{v}) is defined to be the number of these four kinds of dominoes aligning in the way shown in Figure 6. The only difference between these two types is the alignment of the vertical dominoes to the left and the right of dvd_{v}. Overall, we can write the number of domino pairs in TT as

|{domino pairs in ​T}|=∑dv∈V⁡(T)𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏1⁡(dv)=∑dv∈V⁡(T)𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏2⁡(dv).\left|\{\text{domino pairs in }T\}\right|=\sum_{d_{v}\in V(T)}\dinv_{1}(d_{v})=\sum_{d_{v}\in V(T)}\dinv_{2}(d_{v}). (12)

These two expressions will be helpful to compute the dinv statistic later in Section 4.

2.4 Alternating Sign Matrices and Aztec Diamonds

An alternating sign matrix (ASM) of order nn is an n×nn\times n matrix with entries 0,10,1 or −1-1 such that all row and column sums are equal to 11 and the non-zero entries alternate in sign in each row and column. Mills, Robbins, and Rumsey [17] introduced them in the early 1980s. We write ASMn\ASM_{n} for the set of ASMs of order nn. The connection between ASMs and domino tilings of the Aztec diamond was initially discovered in [6, 7]. They showed that the number of domino tilings of the Aztec diamond can be expressed as a weighted enumeration, known as the 22-enumeration of ASMs based on the number of 11’s or −1-1’s in a matrix. The weighted enumeration is given by

|𝒯⁡(ADn)|=∑M∈ASMn2𝖭+​(M)=∑M∈ASMn+12𝖭−​(M),|\T(\AD_{n})|=\sum_{M\in\ASM_{n}}2^{\mathsf{N}_{+}(M)}=\sum_{M\in\ASM_{n+1}}2^{\mathsf{N}_{-}(M)}, (13)

where 𝖭+​(M)\mathsf{N}_{+}(M) (resp., 𝖭−​(M)\mathsf{N}_{-}(M)) is the number of 11’s (resp., −1-1’s) in the matrix MM. This connection was made explicit later by Ciucu [3, Section 2]33 3 In [3, Section 2], this connection was written in the equivalent language of perfect matchings on the planar dual graph of ADn\AD_{n}., the idea is stated as follows.

For two integers xx and yy, we say a (lattice) point (x,y)(x,y) in ADn\AD_{n} is even (resp., odd) if x+yx+y and nn have the same (resp., opposite) parity. For each domino tiling TT of ADn\AD_{n}, we first add four unit segments connecting points (0,n)(0,n) with (0,n+1)(0,n+1), (−n,0)(-n,0) with (−(n+1),0)(-(n+1),0), (0,−n)(0,-n) with (0,−(n+1))(0,-(n+1)), and (n,0)(n,0) with (n+1,0)(n+1,0). Second, we define the maps MeM_{e} and MoM_{o} below.

Me​(ve)={1if deg⁡(ve)=4,0if deg⁡(ve)=3,−1if deg⁡(ve)=2,​ and ​Mo​(vo)={1if deg⁡(vo)=2,0if deg⁡(vo)=3,−1if deg⁡(vo)=4,M_{e}(v_{e})=\begin{cases}1&\text{if $\deg(v_{e})=4$,}\\ 0&\text{if $\deg(v_{e})=3$,}\\ -1&\text{if $\deg(v_{e})=2$,}\end{cases}\text{\quad and \quad}M_{o}(v_{o})=\begin{cases}1&\text{if $\deg(v_{o})=2$,}\\ 0&\text{if $\deg(v_{o})=3$,}\\ -1&\text{if $\deg(v_{o})=4$,}\end{cases} (14)

where deg⁡(⋅)\deg(\cdot) is the degree of an even point vev_{e} or odd point vov_{o} by viewing a domino tiling as a graph. Finally, the image of all even (resp., odd) points under the map MeM_{e} (resp., MoM_{o}) forms a square array (which is an ASM) of size n+1n+1 (resp., nn); see Figures 7 and 7. We write Me​(T)M_{e}(T) and Mo​(T)M_{o}(T) for such ASMs that correspond to TT.

2.5 Domino shuffling

Domino shuffling is first presented in [6, 7] and is used to inductively enumerate domino tilings of ADn\AD_{n}. It is a process that involves moving dominoes in a specific way, we follow closely their idea and summarize some facts about the domino shuffling below.

Recall that we equip ADn\AD_{n} the checkerboard coloring so that the unit squares along the top right side are black. Given a domino tiling TT of ADn\AD_{n}, if we can find a 2×22\times 2 block in TT (consisting of two horizontal or two vertical dominoes), then we say this 2×22\times 2 block is even (resp., odd) if the top right unit square in this block is black (resp., white). An odd-deficient (resp., even-deficient) tiling of TT is obtained from TT by removing all odd (resp., even) blocks of TT.

Domino shuffling is a map SS which sends an odd-deficient tiling ToT_{o} of order nn to an even-deficient tiling Te=S⁡(To)T_{e}=S(T_{o}) of order n+1n+1 by the following actions: (1) slide a vertical domino in which the bottom square is black of ToT_{o} one unit to its left, (2) slide a vertical domino in which the top square is black of ToT_{o} one unit to its right, (3) slide a horizontal domino in which the left square is black of ToT_{o} one unit above it, and (4) slide a horizontal domino in which the right square is black of ToT_{o} one unit below it. We should emphasize that the colors are moved along with dominoes in our case (in [6, 7], the colors are swapped after shuffling, so our terminologies are slightly different from theirs). Figure 8 gives an example of an even-deficient tiling TeT_{e} which is obtained from the odd-deficient tiling ToT_{o} shown in Figure 8 under the domino shuffling.

Suppose that a domino tiling TT of ADn\AD_{n} contains mm odd blocks. The process of sliding dominoes from its odd-deficient tiling ToT_{o} described above opens up some spaces in the Aztec diamond region, these spaces can be filled by m+n+1m+n+1 even blocks. In other words, TeT_{e} has m+n+1m+n+1 even blocks. One can see that the center of an odd (resp., even) block is assigned −1-1 (resp., 11) under the map MeM_{e} (resp., MoM_{o}) described in Section 2.4 since these centers are of degree 22.

Moreover, we define Me​(To)M_{e}(T_{o}) to be the ASM by sending even points of ToT_{o} via the map MeM_{e} and assigning the center of odd blocks to −1-1. Similarly, define Mo​(Te)M_{o}(T_{e}) to be the ASM by sending odd points of TeT_{e} via the map MoM_{o} and assigning the center of even blocks to 11. There is a fact that the ASMs Me​(To)M_{e}(T_{o}) and Mo​(Te)M_{o}(T_{e}) are identical, where TeT_{e} is obtained from ToT_{o} under the domino shuffling. Figure 8 shows the ASM Me​(To)M_{e}(T_{o}) and Mo​(Te)M_{o}(T_{e}), where ToT_{o} is the odd-deficient tiling in Figure 8 while TeT_{e} is the even-deficient tiling in Figure 8. One can see that the −1-1 corresponds to the odd block in Figure 8 and the five 11’s correspond to the five even blocks in Figure 8.

3 Proof of the Nabla Operator Formula

In this section, we first deduce Theorem 1.1 from the Loehr–Warrington formula (as shown in Theorem 2.1). The method of proof is analogous to the deduction of the q,tq,t-Schröder formula from the shuffle formula (see [11, Exercise 6.15]). We then proof the q,tq,t-symmetry of Pλ​(z,q,t)P_{\lambda}(z;q,t) (as shown in Corollary 1.2).

For a weakly-nested λ\lambda-family of Dyck paths π=(πi)\pi=(\pi_{i}), let L⁡(π)L(\pi) denote the set of all labelings of π\pi as in Section 2.2 and define

Fπ=∑w∈L⁡(π)xw​t𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏⁡(π,w).F_{\pi}=\sum_{w\in L(\pi)}x^{w}t^{\dinv(\pi,w)}. (15)

It has been shown that FπF_{\pi} is a symmetric function in {xi}i≥1\{x_{i}\}_{i\geq 1} by writing as a sum of LLT functions ([13, Theorem 2.2]). By Theorem 2.1, FπF_{\pi} satisfies ∇(sλ)=𝗌𝗀𝗇⁡(λ)​∑πq𝖺𝗋𝖾𝖺⁡(π)​Fπ\nabla(s_{\lambda})=\sgn(\lambda)\sum_{\pi}q^{\area(\pi)}F_{\pi}, where the sum is over all weakly-nested λ\lambda-families of Dyck paths.

The weight of a labeling ww of π\pi is the composition 𝗐𝗍⁡(w)=(𝗐𝗍⁡(w)1,𝗐𝗍⁡(w)2,…)\wt(w)=(\wt(w)_{1},\wt(w)_{2},\dots) where 𝗐𝗍⁡(w)i\wt(w)_{i} is the number of ii’s in the labeling ww. We say that a labeling ww of π\pi is called standard if the labels are the numbers 1,2,…,|λ|1,2,\dots,|\lambda| in some order with no repetitions, that is, 𝗐𝗍⁡(w)=(1,…,1,0,…)\wt(w)=(1,\dots,1,0,\dots). Let S​L​(π)SL(\pi) denote the set of standard labelings of π\pi. The reading word of ww, denoted 𝖱𝖾𝖺𝖽⁡(w)\Read(w), is defined by reading the labels appearing in ww along diagonals from top to bottom starting with the diagonal furthest from y=xy=x. For labels on coinciding edges, break ties by reading the labels from the largest indexed path to the smallest, that is, from the weakly innermost path to the weakly outermost path. For example, the reading word of the labeling in Figure 3 is 𝖱𝖾𝖺𝖽⁡(w)=4422131173523\Read(w)=4422131173523.

Given a labeling w∈L⁡(π)w\in L(\pi) (not necessarily standard), the standardization of 𝖱𝖾𝖺𝖽⁡(w)\Read(w) is defined as follows: Replace all the 11’s in 𝖱𝖾𝖺𝖽⁡(w)\Read(w) with the digits 1,2,…,𝗐𝗍⁡(w)11,2,\dots,\wt(w)_{1} in the order they appear in 𝖱𝖾𝖺𝖽⁡(w)\Read(w). Replace all the 22’s in 𝖱𝖾𝖺𝖽⁡(w)\Read(w), not including any change in the previous steps of standardization, with the digits 𝗐𝗍⁡(w)1+1,…,𝗐𝗍⁡(w)1+𝗐𝗍⁡(w)2\wt(w)_{1}+1,\dots,\wt(w)_{1}+\wt(w)_{2} in order. Continuing in this way produces a word in which each digit 1,2,…,|λ|1,2,\dots,|\lambda| appears once each, which we call the standardized reading word of ww, 𝖱𝖾𝖺𝖽′⁡(w)\Read^{\prime}(w).

For example, the standardization of 𝖱𝖾𝖺𝖽⁡(w)=4422131173523\Read(w)=4422131173523, corresponding to the labeling in Figure 3 is 𝖱𝖾𝖺𝖽⁡(w′)=10,11,4,5,1,7,2,3,13,8,12,6,9\Read(w^{\prime})=10,11,4,5,1,7,2,3,13,8,12,6,9. The corresponding standardized labeling w′w^{\prime} is depicted in Figure 9.

Lemma 3.1.

For any labeling w∈L⁡(π)w\in L(\pi), there exists a standard labeling w′∈S​L​(π)w^{\prime}\in SL(\pi) such that the standardization of 𝖱𝖾𝖺𝖽⁡(w)\Read(w) is 𝖱𝖾𝖺𝖽⁡(w′)\Read(w^{\prime}). Moreover, 𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏⁡(π,w)=𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏⁡(π,w′)\dinv(\pi,w)=\dinv(\pi,w^{\prime}).

Proof.

Let w′w^{\prime} be the assignment of labels to the north steps of π\pi from standardization 𝖱𝖾𝖺𝖽′⁡(w)\Read^{\prime}(w) of 𝖱𝖾𝖺𝖽⁡(w)\Read(w) using the same reading order. One easily checks that w′w^{\prime} satisfies the conditions to be a labeling of π\pi from Section 2.2. Indeed, standardization preserves strict inequalities of labels, and in the notation of the second case when r′=rr^{\prime}=r, r′r^{\prime} comes before rr in 𝖱𝖾𝖺𝖽⁡(w)\Read(w) so standardized pair of labels satisfies the required inequality in this case as well.

To verify that 𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏⁡(π,w′)=𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏⁡(π,w)\dinv(\pi,w^{\prime})=\dinv(\pi,w), we observe that any dinv pair for the labeling ww is still a dinv pair for w′w^{\prime}, since the strict inequalities and relative positions between labels are maintained. It remains to check that no new dinv pairs are created from pairs of steps with equal labels in ww but distinct labels in w′w^{\prime}.

Consider two north steps N1N_{1} and N2N_{2} with the same label L1=L2L_{1}=L_{2} in (π,w)(\pi,w) but with distinct labels L1′<L2′L^{\prime}_{1}<L^{\prime}_{2} in (π,w′)(\pi,w^{\prime}), respectively. By the construction of the standardization, L2′L^{\prime}_{2} must be after L1′L^{\prime}_{1} in 𝖱𝖾𝖺𝖽⁡(w′)\Read(w^{\prime}). But dinv pairs always have the larger label on the first step in the reading order (see Figure 4), thus no new dinv pairs are created. ∎

We recall the following definitions from [11, Pages 91 and 99]. For a partition μ\mu of nn, a permutation σ∈Sn\sigma\in S_{n} is called a μ\mu-shuffle if all of the sequences [1,2,…,μ1],[μ1+1,μ1+2,…,μ1+μ2],…[1,2,\dots,\mu_{1}],[\mu_{1}+1,\mu_{1}+2,\dots,\mu_{1}+\mu_{2}],\dots appear as ordered (but not necessarily consecutive) subsequences of σ⁡(1),σ⁡(2),…,σ⁡(n)\sigma(1),\sigma(2),\dots,\sigma(n). For a pair of partitions μ,η\mu,\eta with |μ|+|η|=n|\mu|+|\eta|=n, a permutation σ∈Sn\sigma\in S_{n} is called a μ,η\mu,\eta-shuffle if all of the decreasing sequences [η1,…,1],[η1+η2,…,η1+1],…[\eta_{1},\dots,1],[\eta_{1}+\eta_{2},\dots,\eta_{1}+1],\dots and increasing sequences [|η|+1,…,|η|+μ1],[|η|+μ1+1,…,|η|+μ1+μ2],…[|\eta|+1,\dots,|\eta|+\mu_{1}],[|\eta|+\mu_{1}+1,\dots,|\eta|+\mu_{1}+\mu_{2}],\dots appear as ordered (but not necessarily consecutive) subsequences of σ⁡(1),σ⁡(2),…,σ⁡(n)\sigma(1),\sigma(2),\dots,\sigma(n).

Lemma 3.2.

For any weakly-nested λ\lambda-family Dyck paths π\pi and partition μ\mu with |μ|=|λ||\mu|=|\lambda|, we have

⟨Fπ,hμ⟩=∑w∈S​L​(π)𝖱𝖾𝖺𝖽⁡(w)​ a ​μ​-shufflet𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏⁡(π,w).\langle F_{\pi},h_{\mu}\rangle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}w\in SL(\pi)\\ \Read(w)\text{ a }\mu\text{-shuffle}\end{subarray}}t^{\dinv(\pi,w)}. (16)
Proof.

As mentioned at the beginning of Section 3, FπF_{\pi} is symmetric in {xi}i≥1\{x_{i}\}_{i\geq 1}. Recall that {mμ}\{m_{\mu}\} and {hμ}\{h_{\mu}\} are dual bases of symmetric functions, it turns out that ⟨Fπ,hμ⟩\langle F_{\pi},h_{\mu}\rangle is the coefficient on mμm_{\mu} in the monomial expansion of FπF_{\pi}. Each monomial can be extracted from Fπ=∑w∈L⁡(π)xw​t𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏⁡(π,w)F_{\pi}=\sum_{w\in L(\pi)}x^{w}t^{\dinv(\pi,w)} by fixing the weight of the labeling, giving the expression

⟨Fπ,hμ⟩=∑w∈L⁡(π)𝗐𝗍⁡(w)=μt𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏⁡(π,w).\langle F_{\pi},h_{\mu}\rangle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}w\in L(\pi)\\ \wt(w)=\mu\end{subarray}}t^{\dinv(\pi,w)}. (17)

Then (16) follows from Lemma 3.1 that standardization provides a dinv-preserving bijection between labelings of π\pi of weight μ\mu and standard labelings of π\pi whose reading word is a μ\mu-shuffle. ∎

Now, we are ready to prove Theorem 1.1.

Proof of Theorem 1.1.

By “superization” [11, Theorem 6.10] and Lemma 3.2, for any two partitions μ,η\mu,\eta with |μ|+|η|=|λ||\mu|+|\eta|=|\lambda|, we have

⟨Fπ,hμ​eη⟩=∑w∈S​L​(π)𝖱𝖾𝖺𝖽⁡(w)​ a ​μ,η​-shufflet𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏⁡(π,w).\langle F_{\pi},h_{\mu}e_{\eta}\rangle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}w\in SL(\pi)\\ \Read(w)\text{ a }\mu,\eta\text{-shuffle}\end{subarray}}t^{\dinv(\pi,w)}. (18)

Taking μ=(d)\mu=(d) and η=(n−d)\eta=(n-d), and applying linearity of the Hall inner product to the Loehr–Warrington formula ∇(sλ)=𝗌𝗀𝗇⁡(λ)​∑πq𝖺𝗋𝖾𝖺⁡(π)​Fπ\nabla(s_{\lambda})=\sgn(\lambda)\sum_{\pi}q^{\area(\pi)}F_{\pi} (Theorem 2.1), we therefore obtain

⟨∇(sλ),hd​en−d⟩=𝗌𝗀𝗇⁡(λ)​∑πq𝖺𝗋𝖾𝖺⁡(π)​⟨Fπ,hd​en−d⟩=𝗌𝗀𝗇⁡(λ)​∑(π,w)∈SLNDPλ𝖱𝖾𝖺𝖽⁡(w)​ a ​(d),(n−d)​-shuffleq𝖺𝗋𝖾𝖺⁡(π)​t𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏⁡(π,w).\langle\nabla(s_{\lambda}),h_{d}e_{n-d}\rangle=\sgn(\lambda)\sum_{\pi}q^{\area(\pi)}\langle F_{\pi},h_{d}e_{n-d}\rangle=\sgn(\lambda)\hskip-12.91663pt\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(\pi,w)\in\SLNDP_{\lambda}\\ \Read(w)\text{ a }(d),(n-d)\text{-shuffle}\end{subarray}}\hskip-12.91663ptq^{\area(\pi)}t^{\dinv(\pi,w)}. (19)

The final sum of (19) is over weakly-nested λ\lambda-families of Dyck paths π\pi with standard labeling ww such that 𝖱𝖾𝖺𝖽⁡(w)\Read(w) is a shuffle of the decreasing sequence n−d,…,1n-d,\dots,1 and the increasing sequence n−d+1,…,nn-d+1,\dots,n. We complete the proof by showing that such a pair (π,w)(\pi,w) can be interpreted as a strictly-nested λ\lambda-family of Schröder paths with dd diagonal steps and that the area and dinv statistics of (π,w)(\pi,w) coincide with the statistics on a λ\lambda-family of Schröder paths defined in Section 2.1.

First, we observe that for (π,w)(\pi,w) as above, no two paths in π\pi can share a north step. Indeed, suppose that paths πi\pi_{i} and πj\pi_{j} with i<ji<j share a north step. Since the paths cannot share east steps and cannot intersect at their starting points, the shared north step on πi\pi_{i} is followed by another north step, and the shared north step on πj\pi_{j} is preceded by a north step. Call the labels on these four paths a,b,ca,b,c, and dd in reading order (as shown in Figure 10). By the conditions on labelings in Section 2.2 and the fact that all the labels are distinct since ww is standard, we have inequalities b>a>cb>a>c and b>d>cb>d>c. Subsequences a,b,c,da,b,c,d in 𝖱𝖾𝖺𝖽⁡(w)\Read(w) with these relative order conditions cannot appear in a (d),(n−d)(d),(n-d)-shuffle, since b>a>cb>a>c implies that bb is a part of the increasing sequence n−d+1,…,nn-d+1,\dots,n and cc is a part of the decreasing sequence n−d,…,1n-d,\dots,1, but then there is no way to have b>d>cb>d>c.

Next, we observe that since the labels decrease down each column on any individual path, the sequence n−d+1,…,nn-d+1,\dots,n appearing in increasing order in 𝖱𝖾𝖺𝖽⁡(w)\Read(w) forces any north step with one of these labels to be immediately followed by an east step. We may therefore interpret (π,w)(\pi,w) as a family of Schröder paths by replacing each north step with one of the labels n−d+1,…,nn-d+1,\dots,n and its following east step with a single diagonal step.

The only possible intersections between paths πi\pi_{i} and πj\pi_{j} with i<ji<j is a north step of πi\pi_{i} that starts at the end of a north step of πj\pi_{j}. Call the labels on these paths aa and bb respectively, and note that b>ab>a. Since bb is after aa in 𝖱𝖾𝖺𝖽⁡(w)\Read(w), bb must be a label from the increasing sequence n−d+1,…,nn-d+1,\dots,n. Therefore, when we interpret the step labeled bb and its following east step as a diagonal step, it no longer intersects the path πi\pi_{i}. This shows that the resulting family of Schröder paths is strictly nested. One easily checks that all strictly-nested families of Schröder paths are obtained in this way.

Finally, it is easy to see that the way we obtained a strictly-nested family of Schröder paths mentioned above does not change the area statistic. We also observe that the dinv pairs of vertical and diagonal steps for λ\lambda-families of Schröder paths defined in Section 2.1 coincide with the dinv pairs of labeled weakly-nested Dyck paths whose reading word is a (d),(n−d)(d),(n-d)-shuffle. This completes the proof of Theorem 1.1. ∎

The key point of proving Corollary 1.2 is to show that ∇(sλ)\nabla(s_{\lambda}) is symmetric in qq and tt for any partition λ\lambda. To this end, we state and prove below a more general result [12], which is standard in the study of q,tq,t-Catalan combinatorics and Macdonald polynomials.

Theorem 3.3 ([12]).

Suppose GG is a symmetric function in Λ\Lambda and symmetric in qq and tt. Then ∇(G)\nabla(G) is also symmetric in qq and tt.

Proof.

The Schur expansion of the modified Macdonald polynomials is given by

H~μ​(𝐱,q,t)=∑λ⊢nK~λ,μ​(q,t)​sλ​(𝐱),\tilde{H}_{\mu}(\mathbf{x};q,t)=\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}\tilde{K}_{\lambda,\mu}(q,t)s_{\lambda}(\mathbf{x}), (20)

where K~λ,μ​(q,t)\tilde{K}_{\lambda,\mu}(q,t) is the modified q,tq,t-Kostka polynomial (see [11, Chapter 2]). Using the fact that K~λ,μ​(q,t)=K~λ,μ′​(t,q)\tilde{K}_{\lambda,\mu}(q,t)=\tilde{K}_{\lambda,\mu^{\prime}}(t,q) where μ′\mu^{\prime} denotes the conjugate of μ\mu ([11, Equation (2.30)]), one can readily see that

H~μ​(𝐱,q,t)=H~μ′​(𝐱,t,q).\tilde{H}_{\mu}(\mathbf{x};q,t)=\tilde{H}_{\mu^{\prime}}(\mathbf{x};t,q). (21)

Expressing GG in terms of the modified Macdonald polynomials yields the following:

G\displaystyle G =∑μ⊢naμ​(q,t)​H~μ​(𝐱,q,t)\displaystyle=\sum_{\mu\vdash n}a_{\mu}(q,t)\tilde{H}_{\mu}(\mathbf{x};q,t) (22)
=∑μ⊢naμ′​(q,t)​H~μ′​(𝐱,q,t)\displaystyle=\sum_{\mu\vdash n}a_{\mu^{\prime}}(q,t)\tilde{H}_{\mu^{\prime}}(\mathbf{x};q,t) (23)
=∑μ⊢naμ′​(t,q)​H~μ′​(𝐱,t,q),\displaystyle=\sum_{\mu\vdash n}a_{\mu^{\prime}}(t,q)\tilde{H}_{\mu^{\prime}}(\mathbf{x};t,q), (24)

for some aμ​(q,t)∈ℚ⁡(q,t)a_{\mu}(q,t)\in\mathbb{Q}(q,t). (23) is obtained from (22) by taking the conjugate of each μ\mu and (24) follows from the assumption that GG is symmetric in qq and tt. By (21), we have

aμ​(q,t)=aμ′​(t,q).a_{\mu}(q,t)=a_{\mu^{\prime}}(t,q). (25)

Applying the nabla operator to (22) and using (1), we obtain

∇(G)\displaystyle\nabla(G) =∑μ⊢naμ(q,t)∇(H~μ(𝐱;q,t))\displaystyle=\sum_{\mu\vdash n}a_{\mu}(q,t)\nabla\left(\tilde{H}_{\mu}(\mathbf{x};q,t)\right)
=∑μ⊢naμ​(q,t)​qn⁡(μ′)​tn⁡(μ)​H~μ​(𝐱,q,t).\displaystyle=\sum_{\mu\vdash n}a_{\mu}(q,t)q^{n(\mu^{\prime})}t^{n(\mu)}\tilde{H}_{\mu}(\mathbf{x};q,t). (26)

Taking the conjugate of each μ\mu in (26), by (21) and (25), this shows that ∇(G)\nabla(G) is symmetric in qq and tt. ∎

Proof of Corollary 1.2.

Recall from (3), Pλ​(z,q,t)P_{\lambda}(z;q,t) is the generating polynomial of domino tilings of RλR_{\lambda}, equivalently, the weighted sum of λ\lambda-families of Schröder paths. By Theorem 1.1, we have the following expression.

Pλ​(z,q,t)=𝗌𝗀𝗇⁡(λ)​∑d=0n⟨∇(sλ),hd​en−d⟩​zd.P_{\lambda}(z;q,t)=\sgn(\lambda)\sum_{d=0}^{n}\langle\nabla(s_{\lambda}),h_{d}e_{n-d}\rangle z^{d}. (27)

By Theorem 3.3, ∇(sλ)\nabla(s_{\lambda}) is symmetric in qq and tt for any partition λ\lambda. This implies that ⟨∇(sλ),hd​en−d⟩\langle\nabla(s_{\lambda}),h_{d}e_{n-d}\rangle is symmetric in qq and tt, so is the polynomial Pλ​(z,q,t)P_{\lambda}(z;q,t). ∎

4 Partitions of Square Shape

For the rest of the paper, we continue with the same notations introduced in Section 2. This section focuses on the special case when λ=(nn)\lambda=(n^{n}) (the Ferrers diagram is a square). In Section 4.1, we explain how the region R(nn)R_{(n^{n})} relates to ADn\AD_{n} and provide an example when n=2n=2. We then show how the area (Section 4.2) and dinv (Section 4.3) statistics of a domino tiling of R(nn)R_{(n^{n})} change under the domino shuffling. Finally, the proof of Theorem 1.3 is presented in Section 4.4.

4.1 Extended Aztec Diamonds and Extended ASMs

Decomposing the partition λ=(nn)\lambda=(n^{n}) into border strips gives (n0,n1,…,nk)=(2​k+1,2​k−1,…,3,1)(n_{0},n_{1},\dots,n_{k})=(2k+1,2k-1,\dots,3,1), where k=n−1k=n-1. Recall that in the top half of AD2​n\AD_{2n}, the boxes in the bottom row are labeled as 0,0,1,1,2,2,…,n−1,n−10,0,1,1,2,2,\dots,n-1,n-1 from left to right. The region R(nn)R_{(n^{n})} is formed by removing specific boxes from the bottom row of the top half of AD2​n\AD_{2n}: the white boxes labeled 0,1,…,n−10,1,\dots,n-1 and the black boxes labeled 2​n−1,2​n−2,…,n2n-1,2n-2,\dots,n. In any domino tiling of R(nn)R_{(n^{n})}, vertical dominoes are forced to cover certain parts of the region. After placing these forced vertical dominoes, the remaining region reduces to ADn\AD_{n}. Figure 11 illustrates the border strip decomposition of λ=(44)\lambda=(4^{4}) and Figure 11 shows the region R(44)R_{(4^{4})}, the subregion on the two sides of R(44)R_{(4^{4})} is covered by vertical dominoes. For convenience, the region R(nn)R_{(n^{n})} is referred to as the extended ADn\AD_{n}.

Given a domino tiling TT of the extended ADn\AD_{n}, one can obtain its corresponding extended ASM similarly as in Section 2.4. The idea is to obtain the ASM Me​(T|ADn)M_{e}(T|_{\AD_{n}}) of size n+1n+1 by restricting TT to the region ADn\AD_{n} and then we add a triangular array of 00’s of size nn on the southwestern and southeastern sides, respectively. The resulting extended ASM Me​(T)M_{e}(T) is a triangular array of size 2​n+12n+1. Similarly, the extended ASM Mo​(T)M_{o}(T) can be obtained from Mo​(T|ADn)M_{o}(T|_{\AD_{n}}) of size nn by adding a triangular array of 00’s of size n−1n-1 on the southwestern and southeastern sides, respectively. Sometimes, it will be helpful to view the extended ASMs Me​(T)M_{e}(T) and Mo​(T)M_{o}(T) in this way: we map the even (resp., odd) points within ADn\AD_{n} via MeM_{e} (resp., MoM_{o}), for those even (resp., odd) points outside ADn\AD_{n}, they are all mapped to be 00. Figure 11 provides a domino tiling TT of the extended AD4\AD_{4} and its extended ASM Mo​(T)M_{o}(T). Another example of a domino tiling TT of the extended AD3\AD_{3} and its extended ASM Me​(T)M_{e}(T) is given in Figures 12 and 12.

We would like to point out that the dinv adjustment simplifies to 𝖺𝖽𝗃⁡(λ)=(n2)\adj(\lambda)=\binom{n}{2} when λ=(nn)\lambda=(n^{n}), so the dinv statistic reduces to

𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏⁡(T)=(n2)+|{domino pairs in ​T}|.\dinv(T)=\binom{n}{2}+\left|\{\text{domino pairs in }T\}\right|. (28)
Example 4.1.

In Table 2, we list 88 weighted domino tilings of the extended AD2\AD_{2} where the original AD2\AD_{2} is enclosed by bold edges. One can check that their total weight factors into AD2⁡(z,q,t)=(q​t)2​(z+1)​(z+q)​(z+t)\AD_{2}(z;q,t)=(qt)^{2}(z+1)(z+q)(z+t), which agrees with (5) when n=2n=2.

4.2 Domino shuffling and the area statistic

Given a domino tiling TT of the extended ADn\AD_{n} with mm odd blocks. Let ToT_{o} be the odd-deficient tiling of TT (see Section 2.5) and T^o\hat{T}_{o} be the tiling obtained from ToT_{o} by completing all odd blocks with two horizontal dominoes. We define the area and diags statistics on the odd-deficient tiling ToT_{o} by

𝖺𝗋𝖾𝖺⁡(To)=𝖺𝗋𝖾𝖺⁡(T^o)​ and ​𝖽𝗂𝖺𝗀𝗌⁡(To)=𝖽𝗂𝖺𝗀𝗌⁡(T^o)−m.\area(T_{o})=\area(\hat{T}_{o})\text{ and }\diags(T_{o})=\diags(\hat{T}_{o})-m. (29)

The domino shuffling introduced in Section 2.5 can be applied to an odd-deficient domino tiling ToT_{o} of the extended ADn\AD_{n} similarly. We first attached 2​n2n vertical dominoes at the bottom such that the bottom edges of these 2​n2n vertical dominoes are aligned with the line y=−1y=-1; see the dominoes highlighted in blue in Figure 12 for an example. Next, we apply the domino shuffling process to ToT_{o} and these attached vertical dominoes, and then obtain the even-deficient tiling Te=S⁡(To)T_{e}=S(T_{o}). Figure 12 shows the resulting TeT_{e} under the domino shuffling of ToT_{o} given in Figure 12. Since those forced vertical dominoes on the southwestern (resp., southeastern) side of ADn\AD_{n} are moved one unit to their left (resp., right), creating a space of ADn+1\AD_{n+1} in the middle, this will not lead to conflicts under the domino shuffling process. Similarly, we set T^e\hat{T}_{e} to be the tiling obtained from TeT_{e} by completing m+n+1m+n+1 even blocks with two horizontal dominoes. Define the area and diags statistics on the even-deficient tiling TeT_{e} by

𝖺𝗋𝖾𝖺⁡(Te)=𝖺𝗋𝖾𝖺⁡(T^e)​ and ​𝖽𝗂𝖺𝗀𝗌⁡(Te)=𝖽𝗂𝖺𝗀𝗌⁡(T^e)−(m+n+1).\area(T_{e})=\area(\hat{T}_{e})\text{ and }\diags(T_{e})=\diags(\hat{T}_{e})-(m+n+1). (30)

We show below how the area statistic changes under the domino shuffling.

Proposition 4.2.

Let TT be a domino tiling of the extended ADn\AD_{n} with mm odd blocks, ToT_{o} be the odd-deficient tiling of TT, and Te=S⁡(To)T_{e}=S(T_{o}) be the even-deficient tiling under the domino shuffling of ToT_{o}. Then

𝖺𝗋𝖾𝖺⁡(Te)=𝖺𝗋𝖾𝖺⁡(To)−𝖽𝗂𝖺𝗀𝗌⁡(To)+n⁡(2​n+1)−m.\area(T_{e})=\area(T_{o})-\diags(T_{o})+n(2n+1)-m. (31)

Recall from (10) that the area of a domino tiling TT can be expressed as the sum of 𝖺𝗋𝖾𝖺⁡(dv)\area(d_{v}) and 𝖺𝗋𝖾𝖺⁡(dh)\area(d_{h}) for all vertical dominoes dv∈V⁡(T)d_{v}\in V(T) and horizontal dominoes dh∈H⁡(T)d_{h}\in H(T). To prove Proposition 4.2, we compare the area of dominoes in V⁡(T^o)∪H⁡(T^o)V(\hat{T}_{o})\cup H(\hat{T}_{o}) with the area of dominoes in V⁡(T^e)∪H⁡(T^e)V(\hat{T}_{e})\cup H(\hat{T}_{e}) under the domino shuffling. A central idea is to represent the area of the horizontal domino in each odd or even block as a statistic on the extended ASM Me​(T)M_{e}(T). This statistic is defined as follows: we label the rows of Me​(T)M_{e}(T) from bottom to top by 11 to 2​n+12n+1. If xx is an entry in Me​(T)M_{e}(T) located at row ii, then the level of xx is defined as 𝗅𝖾𝗏𝖾𝗅⁡(x)=i\level(x)=i.

Assuming the bottom edge of the horizontal domino dh∈H⁡(T^o)d_{h}\in H(\hat{T}_{o}) in an odd block is on y=iy=i, this implies that 𝖺𝗋𝖾𝖺⁡(dh)=i\area(d_{h})=i. Also, the center of this odd block corresponds to the entry x=−1x=-1 in the extended ASM Me​(T)M_{e}(T), where 𝗅𝖾𝗏𝖾𝗅⁡(x)=i+1\level(x)=i+1. After the domino shuffling of ToT_{o}, assuming the bottom edge of the horizontal domino dh′∈H⁡(T^e)d^{\prime}_{h}\in H(\hat{T}_{e}) in an even block is on y=jy=j, that is, 𝖺𝗋𝖾𝖺⁡(dh′)=j\area(d^{\prime}_{h})=j. The center of this even block corresponds to the entry y=1y=1 in the same extended ASM, where 𝗅𝖾𝗏𝖾𝗅⁡(y)=j+1\level(y)=j+1. For example, in Figure 12, if we fill the only odd block with two horizontal dominoes, let dhd_{h} be one of these horizontal dominoes in H⁡(T^o)H(\hat{T}_{o}), then the bottom edge of dhd_{h} is on y=4y=4, which implies that 𝖺𝗋𝖾𝖺⁡(dh)=4\area(d_{h})=4. At the same time, this odd block corresponds to the entry x=−1x=-1 shown in Figure 12 and 𝗅𝖾𝗏𝖾𝗅⁡(x)=5\level(x)=5. Similarly, in Figure 12, if we fill the the green-colored even block with two horizontal dominoes, let dh′d^{\prime}_{h} be one of these horizontal dominoes in H⁡(T^e)H(\hat{T}_{e}), then the bottom edge of dh′d^{\prime}_{h} lies on y=3y=3, giving 𝖺𝗋𝖾𝖺⁡(dh′)=3\area(d^{\prime}_{h})=3. This even block corresponds to the entry x=1x=1 highlighted in the green box in Figure 12 and 𝗅𝖾𝗏𝖾𝗅⁡(x)=4\level(x)=4.

Therefore, the area of these particular horizontal dominoes is precisely captured by the level statistic on Me​(T)M_{e}(T). We summarize the above discussion in the following lemma.

Lemma 4.3.

Let TT be a domino tiling of the extended A​DnAD_{n}. Let dh∈H⁡(T^o)d_{h}\in H(\hat{T}_{o}) be a horizontal domino contained in an odd block of T^o\hat{T}_{o} and dh′∈H⁡(T^e)d^{\prime}_{h}\in H(\hat{T}_{e}) be a horizontal domino contained in an even block of T^e\hat{T}_{e}. Let xx be an entry of Me​(T)M_{e}(T) corresponding to the center of an odd or even block. Then

𝗅𝖾𝗏𝖾𝗅⁡(x)−1={𝖺𝗋𝖾𝖺⁡(dh)if x=−1,𝖺𝗋𝖾𝖺⁡(dh′)if x=1.\level(x)-1=\begin{cases}\area(d_{h})&\text{if $x=-1$,}\\ \area(d^{\prime}_{h})&\text{if $x=1$.}\end{cases} (32)

Now, we are prepared to prove Proposition 4.2.

Proof of Proposition 4.2.

Based on (10), (29) and (30), we analyze the area of dominoes in the following two cases: (1) compare the area of dominoes that are not in odd blocks of T^o\hat{T}_{o} with their area contributions after shuffling, and (2) compare the area contributions of odd blocks of T^o\hat{T}_{o} with the area contribution of even blocks of T^e\hat{T}_{e} after shuffling.

Case (1). Let dh∈H⁡(T^o)d_{h}\in H(\hat{T}_{o}) be a horizontal domino that does not belong to any odd block of T^o\hat{T}_{o}. We assume that the bottom edge of dhd_{h} is on y=iy=i, that is, 𝖺𝗋𝖾𝖺⁡(dh)=i\area(d_{h})=i. During the domino shuffling process, this domino is shifted one unit downward. For simplicity, we adjust the yy-coordinate by shifting it downward by one unit, aligning the bottom edge of the resulting even-deficient tiling TeT_{e} with y=0y=0. It turns out that the bottom edge of this domino is still on y=iy=i after shuffling, this implies that 𝖺𝗋𝖾𝖺⁡(dh)\area(d_{h}) does not change after shuffling.

On the other hand, let dv∈V⁡(T^o)d_{v}\in V(\hat{T}_{o}) be a vertical domino that does not belong to any odd block of T^o\hat{T}_{o}. suppose the bottom edge of dvd_{v} is on y=iy=i. During the domino shuffling process, dvd_{v} is shifted one unit to its left. Due to the coordinate adjustment described earlier, the bottom edge of this domino in TeT_{e} is now located at y=i+1y=i+1. Consequently, dvd_{v} contributes one more to the area statistic on TeT_{e} than to ToT_{o}. Therefore, in this case, the additional area contribution under the domino shuffling is equivalent to the number of vertical dominoes in V⁡(T^o)V(\hat{T}_{o}).

Based on the basic counting, the number of dominoes in a domino tiling A∈𝒯⁡(ADn)A\in\T(\AD_{n}) is twice the sum of the number of vertical dominoes in V⁡(A)V(A) and the number of horizontal dominoes in H⁡(A)H(A). This quantity equals to n⁡(n+1)n(n+1). Thus,

|V⁡(A)|=n⁡(n+1)/2−|H⁡(A)|=n⁡(n+1)/2−𝖽𝗂𝖺𝗀𝗌⁡(A).|V(A)|=n(n+1)/2-|H(A)|=n(n+1)/2-\diags(A). (33)

To compute |V⁡(T^o)||V(\hat{T}_{o})|, we restrict T^o\hat{T}_{o} to ADn\AD_{n}. By (29) and (33),

|V⁡(T^o|ADn)|=n⁡(n+1)/2−𝖽𝗂𝖺𝗀𝗌⁡(T^o|ADn)=n⁡(n+1)/2−𝖽𝗂𝖺𝗀𝗌⁡(To|ADn)−m.|V(\hat{T}_{o}|_{\AD_{n}})|=n(n+1)/2-\diags(\hat{T}_{o}|_{\AD_{n}})=n(n+1)/2-\diags(T_{o}|_{\AD_{n}})-m. (34)

Additionally, there are n⁡(n−1)/2n(n-1)/2 forced vertical dominoes in V⁡(To)V(T_{o}) within the extended ADn\AD_{n} that have not yet been accounted for. Therefore, together with (34), the additional area contribution under the domino shuffling in this case is given by

|V⁡(T^o)|=|V⁡(T^o|ADn)|+n⁡(n−1)/2=n2−𝖽𝗂𝖺𝗀𝗌⁡(To)−m.|V(\hat{T}_{o})|=|V(\hat{T}_{o}|_{\AD_{n}})|+n(n-1)/2=n^{2}-\diags(T_{o})-m. (35)

Case (2). Let Hblock​(T^o)H_{\text{block}}(\hat{T}_{o}) (resp., Hblock​(T^e)H_{\text{block}}(\hat{T}_{e})) be the subset of H⁡(T^o)H(\hat{T}_{o}) (resp., H⁡(T^e)H(\hat{T}_{e})) consisting of horizontal dominoes in odd blocks of T^o\hat{T}_{o} (resp., T^e\hat{T}_{e}). By Lemma 4.3, the area of a horizontal domino in Hblock​(T^o)H_{\text{block}}(\hat{T}_{o}) or Hblock​(T^e)H_{\text{block}}(\hat{T}_{e}) can be interpreted by the level statistic of Me​(T)M_{e}(T). As a consequence, the total difference of the area contribution in this case can be written as

∑dh′∈Hblock​(T^e)𝖺𝗋𝖾𝖺⁡(dh′)−∑dh∈Hblock​(T^o)𝖺𝗋𝖾𝖺⁡(dh)=(∑x∈Me​(T)x=1(𝗅𝖾𝗏𝖾𝗅⁡(x)−1))−(∑x∈Me​(T)x=−1(𝗅𝖾𝗏𝖾𝗅⁡(x)−1)).\sum_{d^{\prime}_{h}\in H_{\text{block}}(\hat{T}_{e})}\area(d^{\prime}_{h})-\sum_{d_{h}\in H_{\text{block}}(\hat{T}_{o})}\area(d_{h})=\left(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\in M_{e}(T)\\ x=1\end{subarray}}(\level(x)-1)\right)-\left(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\in M_{e}(T)\\ x=-1\end{subarray}}(\level(x)-1)\right). (36)

It suffices to consider the level statistic on the entries of the original ASM Me​(T|ADn)M_{e}(T|_{\AD_{n}}) of size n+1n+1 (since other entries are 00). From bottom to top, we now label the arrays of Me​(T|ADn)M_{e}(T|_{\AD_{n}}) parallel to y=xy=x by i=1i=1 to i=n+1i=n+1 and the arrays parallel to y=−xy=-x by j=1j=1 to j=n+1j=n+1. It is clear that the level of the entry ai,ja_{i,j} of Me​(T|ADn)M_{e}(T|_{\AD_{n}}) is given by

𝗅𝖾𝗏𝖾𝗅⁡(ai,j)=i+j−1.\level(a_{i,j})=i+j-1. (37)

The key step to evaluate (36) is to identify it as a sum of 𝗅𝖾𝗏𝖾𝗅⁡(ai,j)​ai,j\level(a_{i,j})a_{i,j} over all the entries ai,ja_{i,j} of Me​(T|ADn)M_{e}(T|_{\AD_{n}}) and then simplify it using (37). Then (36) can be rewritten as

∑i,j=1n+1(𝗅𝖾𝗏𝖾𝗅⁡(ai,j)−1)​ai,j\displaystyle\sum_{i,j=1}^{n+1}(\level(a_{i,j})-1)a_{i,j} =∑i,j=1n+1(i+j−2)​ai,j\displaystyle=\sum_{i,j=1}^{n+1}(i+j-2)a_{i,j}
=∑i,j=1n+1i​ai,j+∑i,j=1n+1j​ai,j−2​∑i,j=1n+1ai,j\displaystyle=\sum_{i,j=1}^{n+1}ia_{i,j}+\sum_{i,j=1}^{n+1}ja_{i,j}-2\sum_{i,j=1}^{n+1}a_{i,j}
=∑i=1n+1i​∑j=1n+1ai,j+∑j=1n+1j​∑i=1n+1ai,j−2​∑i,j=1n+1ai,j.\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}i\sum_{j=1}^{n+1}a_{i,j}+\sum_{j=1}^{n+1}j\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}a_{i,j}-2\sum_{i,j=1}^{n+1}a_{i,j}. (38)

Using the fact that each row sum and column sum of an ASM is 11, then (38) reduces to

(n+2)​(n+1)2+(n+2)​(n+1)2−2​(n+1)=n⁡(n+1).\frac{(n+2)(n+1)}{2}+\frac{(n+2)(n+1)}{2}-2(n+1)=n(n+1). (39)

Finally, combining the discussion from these two cases, by (35) and (39),

𝖺𝗋𝖾𝖺⁡(Te)−𝖺𝗋𝖾𝖺⁡(To)\displaystyle\area(T_{e})-\area(T_{o}) =𝖺𝗋𝖾𝖺⁡(T^e)−𝖺𝗋𝖾𝖺⁡(T^o)\displaystyle=\area(\hat{T}_{e})-\area(\hat{T}_{o})
=n2−𝖽𝗂𝖺𝗀𝗌⁡(To)−m+n⁡(n+1)\displaystyle=n^{2}-\diags(T_{o})-m+n(n+1)
=n⁡(2​n+1)−𝖽𝗂𝖺𝗀𝗌⁡(To)−m.\displaystyle=n(2n+1)-\diags(T_{o})-m.

This completes the proof of Proposition 4.2. ∎

4.3 Domino shuffling and the dinv statistic

Given a domino tiling TT of the extended ADn\AD_{n}. Let ToT_{o}, T^o\hat{T}_{o}, TeT_{e}, and T^e\hat{T}_{e} be as in the beginning of Section 4.2. The dinv statistic on an odd-deficient tiling ToT_{o} and even-deficient tiling TeT_{e} are defined as

𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏⁡(To)=𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏⁡(T^o)​ and ​𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏⁡(Te)=𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏⁡(T^e).\dinv(T_{o})=\dinv(\hat{T}_{o})\text{ and }\dinv(T_{e})=\dinv(\hat{T}_{e}). (40)

We show below how the dinv statistic changes under the domino shuffling.

Proposition 4.4.

Given a domino tiling TT of the extended ADn\AD_{n}, let ToT_{o} be the odd-deficient tiling of TT and Te=S⁡(To)T_{e}=S(T_{o}) be the even-deficient tiling under the domino shuffling of ToT_{o}. Then

𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏⁡(Te)=𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏⁡(To)+n2+(n+12).\dinv(T_{e})=\dinv(T_{o})+n^{2}+\binom{n+1}{2}. (41)

As noted in (12), the number of domino pairs in TT can be expressed in two different ways as the sum of the dinv statistic on vertical dominoes in V⁡(T)V(T), depending on the choice of the reference domino in the domino pairs. The main idea of proving Proposition 4.4 is to express the dinv of each vertical domino in V⁡(T^o)V(\hat{T}_{o}) or V⁡(T^e)V(\hat{T}_{e}) as a statistic on the extended ASM Me​(T)M_{e}(T). We introduce the following two statistics on Me​(T)M_{e}(T). Label the rows of Me​(T)M_{e}(T) from bottom to top by 11 to 2​n+12n+1 and let xx be an entry of Me​(T)M_{e}(T) at row ii. The first statistic is called the northeastern sum of xx, denoted by 𝗇𝖾⁡(x)\mathsf{ne}(x), and is defined to be the sum of entries of Me​(T)M_{e}(T) located on the northeastern side of xx (does not include xx itself) along a line parallel to y=xy=x. For example, the second entry x=0x=0 counted from the left at row 11 in Figure 12 has 𝗇𝖾⁡(x)=0+1+0+(−1)+1=1\mathsf{ne}(x)=0+1+0+(-1)+1=1.

The second statistic is called the top partial sum of xx, denoted by 𝗍𝗉⁡(x)\tp(x), and is defined to be the sum of all entries of Me​(T)M_{e}(T) located from the rows i+1i+1 to 2​n+12n+1 and to the right of xx on the same row. For example, let xx be the entry in the green box in Figure 12, and note that xx is located at row 44. Then 𝗍𝗉⁡(x)\tp(x) is the sum of entries located from the rows 55 to 77 and the entries to the right of xx, that is, 𝗍𝗉⁡(x)=0+1+1+0+(−1)+0+0=1\tp(x)=0+1+1+0+(-1)+0+0=1.

Observe that in any domino tiling TT, one of the midpoints of the two longer edges of a domino must be an odd point, while the other midpoint must be an even point. This implies that one of the two midpoints is mapped to an entry of the extended ASM under MeM_{e} or MoM_{o}. An entry xx of the extended ASM Me​(T)M_{e}(T) (or Mo​(T)M_{o}(T)) is said to be associated with a domino in TT if x=Me​(v)x=M_{e}(v) (or Mo​(v)M_{o}(v)), where vv is an even (or odd) point and is the midpoint of the longer edge of that domino. We have seen that at the beginning of the paragraph, for each domino in TT, there exists an entry of Me​(T)M_{e}(T) (or Mo​(T)M_{o}(T)) that is associated with it. We present a result of the statistic 𝗇𝖾⁡(x)\mathsf{ne}(x) in the following lemma, the interested reader can verify it from the example given in Figure 12.

Lemma 4.5.

Let TT be a domino tiling of the extended ADn\AD_{n} and xx be an entry of its extended ASM Me​(T)M_{e}(T) or Mo​(T)M_{o}(T). Then

𝗇𝖾⁡(x)={0, if x=1, 1, if x=−1, 1, if x=0 and x is associated with a domino in V⁡(T)∪H⁡(T). 0, if x=0 and x is associated with a domino in Vc​(T)∪Hc​(T). \mathsf{ne}(x)=\begin{cases}0,&\text{ if $x=1$, }\\ 1,&\text{ if $x=-1$, }\\ 1,&\text{ if $x=0$ and $x$ is associated with a domino in $V(T)\cup H(T)$. }\\ 0,&\text{ if $x=0$ and $x$ is associated with a domino in $V^{c}(T)\cup H^{c}(T)$. }\end{cases} (42)
Proof.

Let v1,v2,…,vdv_{1},v_{2},\dots,v_{d} be the entries of the extended ASM located on the northeastern side of xx along a line parallel to y=xy=x. Note that 𝗇𝖾⁡(x)=∑i=1dvi\mathsf{ne}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{d}v_{i}. According to the definition of the ASM (Section 2.4), it is clear that if x=1x=1, then 𝗇𝖾⁡(x)=0\mathsf{ne}(x)=0, and if x=−1x=-1, then 𝗇𝖾⁡(x)=1\mathsf{ne}(x)=1. When x=0x=0, we prove the lemma for the cases when xx is associated with a vertical domino in V⁡(T)V(T) or in Vc​(T)V^{c}(T); the cases when xx is associated with a horizontal domino in H⁡(T)H(T) or in Hc​(T)H^{c}(T) is omitted here, as they can be addressed in a similar manner.

We proceed with the following two claims.

Claim 1. Assuming x=0x=0 and xx is associated with a vertical domino in V⁡(T)V(T), then there must exist j≤dj\leq d such that vj=1v_{j}=1 and v1=v2=⋯=vj−1=0v_{1}=v_{2}=\cdots=v_{j-1}=0.

Proof of Claim 1.

Figure 13 shows the case when xx is an entry of Me​(T)M_{e}(T) (i.e., the image of an even point under the map MeM_{e}). Let p0,p1,…,pdp_{0},p_{1},\dots,p_{d} be the even points corresponding to x,v1,…,vdx,v_{1},\dots,v_{d}, respectively. In the domino tiling TT, there are four ways to cover the unit square marked XX in Figure 13. For the two cases on the right, deg⁡(p1)=4\deg(p_{1})=4, implying v1=Me​(P1)=1v_{1}=M_{e}(P_{1})=1, and the claim holds. For the two cases on the left, deg⁡(p1)=3\deg(p_{1})=3, giving v1=Me​(Pe)=0v_{1}=M_{e}(P_{e})=0. We then proceed to examine the unit square between p2p_{2} and p3p_{3} in the same way. If v2=1v_{2}=1, the claim holds. If v2=0v_{2}=0, then we continue this process until we find vj=1v_{j}=1 for some j≤dj\leq d. This process will stop: the worst case is when v1=⋯=vd−1=0v_{1}=\cdots=v_{d-1}=0, but this forces vd=1v_{d}=1 since pdp_{d} is on the boundary of the extended ADn\AD_{n} and deg⁡(pd)=4\deg(p_{d})=4.

On the other hand, Figure 13 illustrates the other case when xx is an entry of Mo​(T)M_{o}(T) (i.e., the image of an odd point under the map MoM_{o}). Let q0,q1,…,qdq_{0},q_{1},\dots,q_{d} be the odd points corresponding to x,v1,…,vdx,v_{1},\dots,v_{d}, respectively. In the domino tiling TT, there are three possible ways to cover the unit square marked XX in Figure 13. The leftmost case is not possible because deg⁡(q0)=2\deg(q_{0})=2 which implies x=1x=1 under the map MoM_{o}. For the two cases on the right, deg⁡(q1)<4\deg(q_{1})<4, implying v1≠−1v_{1}\neq-1. We then consider covering the unit square between q1q_{1} and q2q_{2} in a similar way. If this results in v1=1v_{1}=1, then the claim holds. If v1=0v_{1}=0, then this process continues until we find vj=1v_{j}=1 for some j≤dj\leq d. This process will terminate for the same reason described in the previous paragraph: if v1=⋯=vd−1=0v_{1}=\cdots=v_{d-1}=0, then vd=1v_{d}=1. ∎

Claim 2. We assume x=0x=0 and xx is associated with a vertical domino in Vc​(T)V^{c}(T). If there exists j≤dj\leq d such that vj≠0v_{j}\neq 0 and v1=v2=⋯=vj−1=0v_{1}=v_{2}=\cdots=v_{j-1}=0, then vj=−1v_{j}=-1.

Proof of Claim 2.

We assume the contrary that vj=1v_{j}=1. Figure 14 shows the case when xx is an entry of Me​(T)M_{e}(T). Let p0,p1,…,pjp_{0},p_{1},\dots,p_{j} be the even points corresponding to x,v1,…,vjx,v_{1},\dots,v_{j}, respectively. We have deg⁡(pj)=4\deg(p_{j})=4 and deg⁡(pi)=3\deg(p_{i})=3 for i=1,…,j−1i=1,\dots,j-1. As a consequence, in the domino tiling TT, there are two ways to cover the unit square marked XX in Figure 14 and the edges of dominoes must contain the “southwestern hook” of each pip_{i} for i=1,…,j−1i=1,\dots,j-1, that is, the union of the two edges pointing west and south from pip_{i}. It turns out that there is only one way to cover the unit square between xx and v1v_{1} which makes deg⁡(p0)=2\deg(p_{0})=2 and x=Me​(p0)=−1x=M_{e}(p_{0})=-1, this contradicts to the assumption that x=0x=0.

Figure 14 shows the other case when xx is an entry of Mo​(T)M_{o}(T). Let q0,q1,…,qjq_{0},q_{1},\dots,q_{j} be the odd points corresponding to x,v1,…,vjx,v_{1},\dots,v_{j}, respectively. We have deg⁡(qj)=2\deg(q_{j})=2 and deg⁡(qi)=3\deg(q_{i})=3 for i=1,…,j−1i=1,\dots,j-1. Consequently, in the domino tiling TT, there are two ways to cover the unit square marked XX in Figure 14 and the edges of dominoes must contain the “northeastern hook” of each qiq_{i} for i=1,…,j−1i=1,\dots,j-1. This leads to deg⁡(q1)=4\deg(q_{1})=4 and v1=Mo​(q1)=−1v_{1}=M_{o}(q_{1})=-1, which violates the assumption that v1=0v_{1}=0. ∎

If x=0x=0 and xx is associated with a vertical domino in V⁡(T)V(T), then Claim 1 implies that

𝗇𝖾⁡(x)=∑i=1j−1vj+vj+𝗇𝖾⁡(vj)=0+1+0=1.\mathsf{ne}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{j-1}v_{j}+v_{j}+\mathsf{ne}(v_{j})=0+1+0=1.

Finally, when x=0x=0 and xx is associated with a vertical domino in Vc​(T)V^{c}(T), if all the viv_{i}’s are 00, then 𝗇𝖾⁡(x)=0\mathsf{ne}(x)=0. If not, then Claim 2 implies that

𝗇𝖾⁡(x)=∑i=1j−1vj+vj+𝗇𝖾⁡(vj)=0+(−1)+1=0.\mathsf{ne}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{j-1}v_{j}+v_{j}+\mathsf{ne}(v_{j})=0+(-1)+1=0.

This completes the proof of Lemma 4.5. ∎

Before stating the result of the second statistic 𝗍𝗉\tp, we partition the set V⁡(T)=Vg​(T)∪Vb​(T)V(T)=V_{g}(T)\cup V_{b}(T), where Vg​(T)V_{g}(T) consists of vertical dominoes lying on the ground (i.e., the bottom edge of a domino lies on y=0y=0) and are not in ADn\AD_{n}, and Vb​(T)=V⁡(T)∖Vg​(T)V_{b}(T)=V(T)\setminus V_{g}(T). Notice that for a domino tiling TT of the extended ADn\AD_{n}, |Vg​(T)|=n−1|V_{g}(T)|=n-1. In the following lemma, the relation between statistics 𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏1\dinv_{1}, 𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏2\dinv_{2} (Section 2.3) and 𝗍𝗉\tp is presented.

Lemma 4.6.

Given a domino tiling TT of the extended ADn\AD_{n}, let dvd_{v} be a vertical domino in the set Vb​(T)V_{b}(T). Suppose the entry xx of Me​(T)M_{e}(T) and the entry yy of Mo​(T)M_{o}(T) are associated with dvd_{v}. Note that x=0​ or −1x=0\text{ or }-1 under the map MeM_{e}, and y=0​ or ​1y=0\text{ or }1 under the map MoM_{o}. Then

𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏1⁡(dv)=𝗍𝗉⁡(x)−1​ and ​𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏2⁡(dv)=𝗍𝗉⁡(y)−δy,0,\dinv_{1}(d_{v})=\tp(x)-1\text{ and }\dinv_{2}(d_{v})=\tp(y)-\delta_{y,0}, (43)

where δ\delta denotes the Kronecker delta function.

Proof.

Since dv∈Vb​(T)d_{v}\in V_{b}(T), the four configurations of the domino pair with dvd_{v} may exist in TT. The situation when dv∈Vg​(T)d_{v}\in V_{g}(T) will be discussed in Remark 4.7. We consider the first case when xx is the entry of Me​(T)M_{e}(T) and is on the line ℓ2\ell_{2}; see Figure 15 for an illustration. In this case, x=−1x=-1 or x=0x=0, hence 𝗇𝖾⁡(x)=1\mathsf{ne}(x)=1. Viewing dvd_{v} as the type I reference domino (Figure 6), we proceed with the following claim about the statistic 𝗇𝖾\mathsf{ne} and domino pairs.

Claim 3. Let uu be an entry of Me​(T)M_{e}(T) on the line ℓ2\ell_{2} and the left of dvd_{v}, or on the line ℓ1\ell_{1} and the right of dvd_{v}. Then the domino that uu is associated with forms a domino pair with dvd_{v} if and only if 𝗇𝖾⁡(u)=1\mathsf{ne}(u)=1.

Proof of Claim 3.

We discuss the following three possible values of uu.

  • •

    u=−1u=-1. Since uu corresponds to an odd block in TT filled by two horizontal or two vertical dominoes, in either case, one of the dominoes forms a domino pair with dvd_{v} (such as the dominoes that s1s_{1} and r1r_{1} are associated with in Figure 15), contributing 11 to the 𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏1\dinv_{1} statistic. Lemma 4.5 implies 𝗇𝖾⁡(u)=1\mathsf{ne}(u)=1.

  • •

    u=0u=0. If uu is associated with a domino which forms a domino pair with dvd_{v} (such as the dominoes that s2s_{2} and r2r_{2} are associated with in Figure 15), that is, they belong to the set V⁡(T)∪H⁡(T)V(T)\cup H(T), then Lemma 4.5 implies 𝗇𝖾⁡(u)=1\mathsf{ne}(u)=1. On the other hand, if uu is associated with a domino which does not form a domino pair with dvd_{v} (for example, the dominoes that s3s_{3} and r3r_{3} are associated with in Figure 15), that is, they belong to the set Vc​(T)∪Hc​(T)V^{c}(T)\cup H^{c}(T), then 𝗇𝖾⁡(u)=0\mathsf{ne}(u)=0 by Lemma 4.5.

  • •

    u=1u=1. The even point corresponding to uu has degree 44, drawn as s4s_{4} and r4r_{4} in Figure 15. No matter how we place dominoes incident to this even point, none of them forms a domino pair with dvd_{v}. By Lemma 4.5, 𝗇𝖾⁡(u)=0\mathsf{ne}(u)=0.

From the above discussion, we see that uu is associated with a domino that forms a domino pair with dvd_{v} if and only if 𝗇𝖾⁡(u)=1\mathsf{ne}(u)=1. ∎

In this case, we observe that the top partial sum of xx can be written as

𝗍𝗉⁡(x)=𝗇𝖾⁡(x)+∑u𝗇𝖾⁡(u),\tp(x)=\mathsf{ne}(x)+\sum_{u}\mathsf{ne}(u),

where uu runs over all the entries of Me​(T)M_{e}(T) on ℓ2\ell_{2} and the left of dvd_{v} or on ℓ1\ell_{1} and the right of dvd_{v}. By Claim 3, 𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏1⁡(dv)=𝗍𝗉⁡(x)−𝗇𝖾⁡(x)=𝗍𝗉⁡(x)−1\dinv_{1}(d_{v})=\tp(x)-\mathsf{ne}(x)=\tp(x)-1.

Now, we look at the second case when yy is the entry of Mo​(T)M_{o}(T) and is on the line ℓ2\ell_{2}; see Figure 15 for an illustration. In this case, y=1y=1 or y=0y=0, hence 𝗇𝖾⁡(y)=δy,0\mathsf{ne}(y)=\delta_{y,0}. Viewing dvd_{v} as the type II reference domino (Figure 6), we proceed similarly with the following claim.

Claim 4. Let uu be an entry of Mo​(T)M_{o}(T) on the line ℓ2\ell_{2} and the right of dvd_{v}, or on the line ℓ3\ell_{3} and the left of dvd_{v}. Then the domino that uu is associated with forms a domino pair with dvd_{v} if and only if u+𝗇𝖾⁡(u)=1u+\mathsf{ne}(u)=1.

Proof of Claim 4.

We similarly analyze the three possible values of uu, as follows:

  • •

    u=1u=1. Since uu corresponds to an even block in TT filled by two horizontal or two vertical dominoes, in either case, one of the dominoes forms a domino pair with dvd_{v} (such as the dominoes that s5s_{5} and r5r_{5} are associated with in Figure 15), contributing 11 to the 𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏2\dinv_{2} statistic. Lemma 4.5 implies u+𝗇𝖾⁡(u)=1u+\mathsf{ne}(u)=1.

  • •

    u=0u=0. If uu is associated with a domino which forms a domino pair with dvd_{v} (such as the dominoes that s6s_{6} and r6r_{6} are associated with in Figure 15), that is, they belong to the set V⁡(T)∪H⁡(T)V(T)\cup H(T), then Lemma 4.5 implies u+𝗇𝖾⁡(u)=1u+\mathsf{ne}(u)=1. On the other hand, if uu is associated with a domino which does not form a domino pair with dvd_{v} (for example, the dominoes that s7s_{7} and r7r_{7} are associated with in Figure 15), that is, they belong to the set Vc​(T)∪Hc​(T)V^{c}(T)\cup H^{c}(T), then u+𝗇𝖾⁡(u)=0u+\mathsf{ne}(u)=0 by Lemma 4.5.

  • •

    u=−1u=-1. The odd point corresponding to uu has degree 44, shown as s8s_{8} and r8r_{8} in Figure 15. No matter how we place dominoes incident to this odd point, none of them forms a domino pair with dvd_{v}. By Lemma 4.5, u+𝗇𝖾⁡(u)=0u+\mathsf{ne}(u)=0.

From the above discussion, Claim 4 holds. ∎

In this case, 𝗍𝗉⁡(y)\tp(y) is slightly different from 𝗍𝗉⁡(x)\tp(x) mentioned in the first case, it is given by

𝗍𝗉⁡(y)=𝗇𝖾⁡(y)+∑u(u+𝗇𝖾⁡(u)),\tp(y)=\mathsf{ne}(y)+\sum_{u}(u+\mathsf{ne}(u)),

where uu runs over all the entries of Mo​(T)M_{o}(T) on ℓ3\ell_{3} and the left of dvd_{v} or on ℓ2\ell_{2} and the right of dvd_{v}. By Claim 4, 𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏2⁡(dv)=𝗍𝗉⁡(y)−𝗇𝖾⁡(y)=𝗍𝗉⁡(y)−δy,0\dinv_{2}(d_{v})=\tp(y)-\mathsf{ne}(y)=\tp(y)-\delta_{y,0}. This completes the proof of Lemma 4.6. ∎

Remark 4.7.

Let T,x,yT,x,y be the same as in Lemma 4.6. The identity 𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏1⁡(dv)=𝗍𝗉⁡(x)−1\dinv_{1}(d_{v})=\tp(x)-1 does not hold for dv∈Vg​(T)d_{v}\in V_{g}(T). The issue arises when viewing dvd_{v} as the type I reference domino, one of the configurations of the domino pairs involving dvd_{v} does not exist in TT (see the vertical domino that r2r_{2} is associated with in Figure 15), and this discrepancy is not accurately reflected in Me​(T)M_{e}(T). Hence, 𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏1⁡(dv)<𝗍𝗉⁡(x)−1\dinv_{1}(d_{v})<\tp(x)-1. However, if we attach 2​n2n vertical dominoes at the bottom of TT (like the dominoes highlighted in blue in Figure 12), then this does give the correct identity 𝖽𝗂𝗇𝗏1⁡(dv)=𝗍𝗉⁡(x)−1\dinv_{1}(d_{v})=\tp(x)-1 for dv∈Vg​(T)d_{v}\in V_{g}(T). On the other hand, all four configurations of the domino pairs could exist when viewing dvd_{v} as the type II reference domino.
